The E-3 group is a trio of European powers — France, Britain and Germany — that was set up more than 20 years ago to advance diplomatic coordination over Iran’s nuclear programme. The Foreign Office in Islamabad has yet to comment on the planned meetings and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar’s participation. A Turkish diplomatic source told Reuters that the seven countries would meet in the R-4+E-3 format for the first time at Turkiye’s initiative as wars involving Iran , Yemen and Ukraine threaten shipping routes and regional security. The ministers are expected to discuss the Israeli-Palestinian issue, the latest situation in the Strait of Hormuz, developments related to Yemen, efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war, and opportunities for closer cooperation between the regional and European countries, the source added. Fidan is expected to emphasise the need for a diplomatic solution to the war between the United States and Iran, the importance of freedom of navigation in the straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, and reiterate Turkiye’s support for Saudi Arabia’s security against attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed by Islamabad, Ankara, and Riyadh, they said. Fidan will also tell counterparts that Turkiye has been working to stop the war in Ukraine from spreading to the Black Sea, pointing to the regional security risks posed by the conflict, the source said.

title: England's Brook hits record ODI double ton but Sri Lanka pull off epic chase in Rawalpindi clash
description: England’s Harry Brook smashed the fastest double-century in One-Day International (ODI) history and became the first Englishman to score 200 in the format but Sri Lanka sealed a two-wicket win in their tri-series clash with one ball to spare in Rawalpindi on Thursday. The 27-year-old captain rewrote the record books by racing to his double hundred in 114 balls, surpassing the previous mark of 117 deliveries set by India’s Shubman Gill. In the process, Brook also eclipsed England’s highest individual ODI score of 182, held by all-rounder Ben Stokes. Brook’s scintillating performance ended with the final ball of England’s innings when he was caught by Sahan Arachchige off the bowling of Janith Liyanage. England’s captain Harry Brook celebrates after scoring a double century (200 runs) during the one-day international (ODI) tri-series cricket match between England and Sri Lanka at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium in Rawalpindi on October 22, 2026. — AFP He made 202 from 116 deliveries, peppering the Sri Lanka attack with 21 fours and 10 sixes before departing to warm applause from the crowd. The defeat leaves England bottom of the standings after losing both their matches, with Brook saying they need to win their next two games to reach the final in Lahore. “Unfortunately, it (the record) doesn’t matter now. I thought we were going to be in a good position but, unfortunately, it doesn’t even count,” Brook said. “Heart-breaking. I think you’ve hit the nail on the head there. It’s very disappointing that we haven’t been able to defend 430, but that’s life, that’s cricket,” he added. “You don’t see many teams chase down 430 and hats off to Sri Lanka. They’ve played exceptionally well. We couldn’t execute our skills enough with the ball and, again, they’ve just played an absolute blinder there. “We’ll have a good chat about it now and over the next couple of days. We’ve got a good opportunity in the next couple of games to really try and get to that final in Lahore.” Joe Root provided strong support with 69 off 66 balls as England piled up 429-4. But the total proved insufficient as Sri Lanka completed the second-highest successful run chase in ODI history. Pavan Rathnayake top-scored with 130 from 106 deliveries, while opener Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka both fell three runs short of centuries. Sri Lanka’s Pavan Rathnayake in action in the one-day international (ODI) tri-series cricket match between England and Sri Lanka at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium in Rawalpindi on October 22, 2026. — Reuters Needing six runs from the final two deliveries, Sri Lanka sealed victory when Liyanage launched Josh Tongue over long-off for six, leaving Brook’s record-breaking innings all in vain. Tongue was England’s most successful bowler with 3-79. England lost by 87 runs at the same venue in Rawalpindi on Tuesday to Pakistan, who lead the table with two wins from two.

title: Welfarism is dead
description: PARADED as amongst the greatest achievements of ‘advanced’ capitalist countries in the post-World War II period, the welfare state epitomised an era of widespread social prosperity. The mass of people in Western Europe, North America, and Australasia was largely guaranteed public education, healthcare, water, electricity, and other material needs. Working-age populations either found work in bustling manufacturing industries or received significant unemployment benefits. The anti-communist US ideologue, Walt Rostow, boasted that the ‘West’ had successfully entered the age of high mass consumption. Today, as mass protests rock France, the welfare state can officially be pronounced dead. The convulsions were triggered by high school and university students demanding accountability for the rapidly deteriorating and underfunded education sector. The demise extends to all spheres of life, and to all parts of the so-called developed world. The welfare state itself was not a gift from above but a compulsion forced upon ruling classes of Western countries petrified of working-class populations at home and colonised people demanding self-rule in Asia and Africa. The fear was that the masses would be taken in by the irrepressible appeal of Soviet, and later, Chinese socialism. Seen thus, the welfare state represented a historic compromise between capital and labour. The former accepted regulation of profits, progressive taxation, and limits on its political power; the latter took on the role of an empowered citizenry that would eschew revolutionary politics. It is no surprise that the unravelling of this capital-labour compact coincided to a significant extent with the collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of the Cold War. The balance of class forces within Western societies had already started to shift with the emergence of what later became known as neoliberalism in the late 1970s, but the die was cast by the end of actually existing socialism. The demise extends to all spheres. It has been a slow death, because welfare apparatuses do not disappear overnight; neither do people’s expectations of the state. Indeed, what is happening in France today is itself a reflection that the mass of the people deeply imbibed ideas of citizenship during the era of welfarism. Compared to our society, students, workers, and other social forces in countries like France are still well-organised and possess the ability and will to rock the system. Nevertheless, the unleashing of neoliberal capital and the attendant rollback of public funding in health, education, and other public infrastructure have had devastating effects. Stagnating real incomes, growing inequality, and an overall decline in social well-being have been feasted on by hate-mongering right-wing forces, while entities like the British Labour Party and French Socialist Party have totally abandoned the left project. The shameful retreat of social democratic parties aside, the welfare state will not return because the historical conjuncture that spawned it is over. The reconstruction of war-ravaged Britain and France from the late 1940s was funded by Washington through the so-called Marshall Plan; post-Nazi West Germany was also given an economic foothold in world trade because of US largesse. The US empire is no longer willing to prop up Europe; it is also drastically cutting aid to the so-called developing world. It’s worth being reminded that the zenith of the welfare state in ‘advanced’ capitalist countries was coeval with either aid dependency, violent coups, or imperialist wars in the erstwhile Third Wo­­rld. Think Pakistan under Ayub Khan, or Vietnam, the Congo and Chile. A few Third World countries broke with the dominant trend, notably the East Asian ‘developmental state’. Some, like South Korea, benefited from being central to Washington’s Cold War designs, their infant industries given preferential access to the US market. But state apparatuses were authoritarian, and there were fewer concessions made to labouring classes by capitalist interests in comparison to the Western prototype. We in Pakistan have never really had a welfarist interregnum. When socialism was a mass ideology in the 1960s and 1970s, governing regimes adopted a few tangible policies like land reforms and nationalisation. But the state remained colonial in its orientation and was never fully subdued to the public interest. Today, like many of its counterparts, the Pakistani state couldn’t care less about the masses’ welfare. Profit and repression are its only concerns. When mass protests do erupt, structural change remains elusive. A new era of mass prosperity to transcend the historical inheritance of the capitalist world system requires both ideology and organisation. Only then can we force the state and capital into retreat. The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: How to sustain research?
description: IN terms of urgent and important problems requiring resolution, Pakistan’s education sector is the real frontier. With some 26 million five- to 16-year-olds out of school, a lack of universal enrolment, high dropout rates, and the poor quality of education provided to most of those lucky enough to be enrolled, could any issue be more important? Pakistan has a very young population; we are still growing at 2.4 per cent every year. This means that approximately 6m children are added to the population annually. In more developed societies, the frontiers are about ageing populations and health. In Pakistan, they are about children, their schooling and health; young people and their education and skills; and early employment opportunities. All this implies that Pakistan provides a research frontier for those interested in education. And we need a lot of research. We face big questions and need good answers: how can we provide education to millions; how do we improve the quality of education; how do we manage private versus public schools; how do we recruit, train, and support teachers; how do we govern and manage schools and systems better; how do we ensure good curricula, books, assessments, teaching, etc? The list is long; we need good research to answer all these questions and more. But, historically — and even today — education research has not been a priority area for funding. First, the education sector, as a whole, has always been underfunded. Even in better days, the state never spent more than 2pc of GDP on education; currently, we are at less than 1pc. Within this, one can imagine what funding for research would be and what, within research funding, funding for education research must have been. Second, there are strong biases in research funding agencies, such as the Higher Education Commission, for research in science and technology as against research in the social sciences, humanities and the arts. The general thinking is that Pakistan needs engineers and technologists — and thus research in science and technology for development. Research in the social sciences, humanities, and the arts is not seen as important or needed, nor is it viewed as providing the returns that society needs. Historically, research done on education in Pakistan was conducted either locally — with smaller budgets and samples — by academics and students in university education programmes, or by foreign academics and academics based abroad. The latter had higher budgets. A lot of the research was funded by multilateral and bilateral agencies such as the World Bank, DFID (now FCDO — the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office), USAID, GIZ, etc. A lot of the local research was not published internationally, while international work did little or nothing to develop local capacity. Some good partnerships developed between local and international academics, but these were rare and tended not to last beyond the life of the project. Education research has not been a priority area for funding. It has been interesting to follow the Data and Research in Education — Research Consortium (DARE-RC) in this context. This FCDO-funded programme, due to end by December, tried to change the existing equilibrium. The main ingredients of change were the following: a) it encouraged local researchers to apply for competitive funding; b) it encouraged collaborations across local institutions; c) it encouraged collaborations across local and international academics and institutions as well; d) it committed to making all data public; and e) it insisted on quality outputs that should be published internationally. More than 40 different studies were commissioned; many of them have been completed and their reports and policy briefs are available. Some of the early studies have already been slated for publication in international journals, while many are in the process of being submitted. Some will be appearing in a special issue of an international journal. Many interesting partnerships have been created among local universities, between universities and research institutions, between local and international researchers, and between local and international universities. This has led to quite a bit of capacity building, and has provided each project with junior research assistants. Quite a few people have been trained and mentored over the last few years. There has been considerable interaction with policymakers and the wider public, with one or two DARE-RC events held every couple of weeks this year. DARE-RC has even started a yearly conference on education. The second edition is at the end of the month in Lahore. But there are issues too. As DARE-RC winds down and the funding ends, it appears that, given the new global funding realities, FCDO is not going to support such programmes anymore. What happens to the gains made? Will the collaborations be sustained? Will someone take over the yearly conference? Will the fora created for capacity building and sharing research continue beyond DARE-RC funding? Will the sharing of data for research continue? Will cooperation between researchers and policymakers continue? Or will it lapse as it has on previous occasions? Will the government, federal or provincial education departments, or HEC take on the role of research funder? The research has been very policy-focused and has helped in critical areas such as teacher recruitment and licensing, inclusive education, improved teaching and learning in classrooms, education and support for children with disabilities, and curricula and textbook improvements. Do departments see value in such research, and will they provide support for sustaining and expanding the networks that have been created? Research is the backbone of progress, but quality research is expensive, hard to do, and even harder to sustain. We urgently need a lot of high-quality research in education. Recent investments, through DARE-RC in particular, have provided insights and lessons on how networks capable of producing the high-quality research needed to improve education outcomes can be created. But will these gains be sustainable beyond the life of the project? What will continue and what will not? A lot depends on whether the HEC or the education departments come forward to support and expand the current networks. The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Nuclear uncertainty
description: CONSIDERING the poor state of bilateral relations between Pakistan and India, there is always a possibility of miscalculating a situation, especially in the absence of regular contact. These concerns take on greater importance in the nuclear domain. In this regard, officials associated with Pakistan’s nuclear programme have rightly warned that India’s reported attempt to alter the strategic balance has heightened risks of escalation in South Asia. Speaking at a conference in Islamabad, retired Lt-Gen Khalid Kidwai, adviser to the National Command Authority, highlighted a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, which said that India had deployed nuclear warheads on a submarine as part of “deterrence patrols”. He also cited New Delhi’s lack of advance notification for ballistic missile tests. The official observed that these developments cast doubt on India’s no-first-use policy, and were seen as an “irresponsible escalatory transition” towards nuclear asymmetry. Lack of coordination between nuclear states creates great unknowns, and such a situation is untenable in a neighbourhood as volatile as South Asia. It should be remembered that it was only last year that Pakistan and India confronted each other on the battlefield, illustrating how quickly matters can escalate. In such an atmosphere, India’s apparent attempts to alter the strategic balance are cause for serious concern. As Lt-Gen Kidwai pointed out, Pakistan may “review and reconsider” its deployment options, while reminding New Delhi of this country’s full spectrum deterrence policy. With matters frozen in the political and diplomatic spheres, it will take military-to-military engagement to prevent miscalculation in the strategic sphere. This can be carried out through the directors general military operations hotline, or via other appropriate channels. India’s political class — as well as military officials — has issued jingoistic statements targeting Pakistan. There is certainly no room for such bluster where the issue of nuclear weapons is concerned. To ward off any potential catastrophe, the situation must be handled in a rational manner and lines of communication need to be kept open to ensure conventional or nuclear signals are not misconstrued. India should halt its highly provocative nuclear-armed submarine patrols and engage with Pakistan to ensure there are no misunderstandings, particularly in the strategic sphere. Regular diplomatic engagement may seem distant at this juncture, but contact between the defence command structures should continue, while de-escalation mechanisms should also be maintained. Most of all, India should give up its rash attitude and approach the issue with maturity if it wants to reduce tensions and advance regional peace. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Game Review — Marvel’s Wolverine just doesn't make the cut
description: TL;DR Pros: Wolverine is a comic-accurate short king Highly detailed facial capture and character models Visceral, stylish and satisfying combat … at first Voice acting is decent, even if the material isn’t Stunning set-pieces Cons: Why is there a blue line permanently guiding me through a level with only one path? Combat can feel barebones and repetitive at times “Hidden” collectables are exposed by very invasive visual cues Stealth and boss fights are awful Score: 4/7 — Not worth buying at full price. Play it when it eventually lands on PlayStation Plus. Reviewed on PlayStation 5; available on PlayStation 5 Price: Rs18,000 (physical copy), $69.99 ( PlayStation Store ) All screenshots and GIFs captured by author. If you’ve read my reviews, you’ll likely know I’m a big DC and Marvel fan, and games like Batman Arkham and the Spider-Man series hold a special place in my heart. I wrote a two-parter on Lego Batman for heaven’s sake. So when Insomniac, the minds behind PlayStation’s Spider-Man series, announced that they were developing a Wolverine game, I was genuinely hyped. Spider-Man gave us engaging combat, vibrant worlds to explore and, especially in the case of the first title, amazing stories to tell. It was a first-party Sony exclusive. What could go wrong? As it so happens, quite a fair bit. Marvel’s Wolverine has a decent foundation, but there’s barely any meat on the adamantium skeleton. A solid, but shallow, combat system gets repetitive, and the game is extremely linear, but for some reason, it doesn’t believe you can proceed through missions without a blue line festooned upon the screen guiding you. While that description may sound harsh, let’s be clear: Wolverine isn’t a bad game; there’s far worse stuff out there that you and I have played. But this is absolutely not worth the full price of admission. Let’s jump in and see why, motorbike and all. I won’t lie, this bit was pretty cool. Skin deep? Off the bat, I want to talk about what the game gets right before diving into what brings it down, starting with the presentation. The game looks genuinely impressive, with Tokyo, the Canadian wilderness and Madripoor’s Lowtown neighbourhood truly standing out with unique aesthetics and a high level of environmental detail. Shinjuku has never looked this good. The same goes for (some) of the character models, with incredible facial capture which depicts microexpressions and the likenesses of the actors perfectly; at times, the characters are genuinely lifelike. Why the long face, Logan? They’re also voiced well; Liam McIntyre does an especially good job as the eponymous hero and capturing his anger, and whenever he roars, I definitely hear Logan, aka Wolverine. He also stands out in particular due to his appearance after being injured. When taking damage, his skin will be removed, exposing the adamantium skeleton underneath, much like the Uncaged Edition of 2009’s X-Men Origins: Wolverine but with higher visual fidelity. Wounds also heal in real-time, not only looking cool but also showcasing the iconic mutant’s powers. It was at this point the thugs knew they goofed up. Scripted sequences in the story are bombastic and, as the game goes on, massive in scale. Sequences with a plane over Tokyo and a casino stood out to me in particular. So it looks superb, as one would expect from a full-price AAA blockbuster, but that only goes skin deep. Once you dig through the first layer, it becomes clear that the presentation is as wide as an ocean but as deep as a puddle. The sprawling Canadian wilderness is limited to only two or three very linear paths. Invisible walls prevent you from exploring Tokyo’s Shinjuku area. Locations like labs look absolutely soulless compared to the others. The first mission sees you claw your way through one, and I did not like the aesthetic, or lack thereof. Granted, this was never meant to be an open-world game, but a bit more freedom to explore wouldn’t have hurt, and no-go areas could have been blocked off with objects rather than an invisible barrier. The strongest points of the level design are when you can explore and find hidden collectables, or items like documents and voice recordings to flesh out the game’s lore. More style than substance. What a shame. Rip and tear, until it is done The game’s combat system is something that initially had me excited, and indeed, it’s a solid system with a strong foundation. But upon getting the claws out, one thing becomes very clear: the combat system is a restricted version of Spider-Man’s . You just spam the square button to hit enemies, circle to dodge and L1 to parry attacks, just like Spider-Man . Obviously, it’s far more brutal due to the game’s darker tone, but provides an incredible spectacle, especially against the backdrop of some of the game’s environments. THIS IS CANADA. This is aided by destructible props that will completely fall to pieces once Logan goes to town. Wooden boards, street carts and other objects will completely splinter apart. Everything put together is absolutely glorious. It is genuinely fun at times to engage groups of enemies in this game, building up the rage meter and using special moves, with Logan’s roar and the clash of steel filling your ears. It’s in these moments where the game is at its strongest. However, the combat quickly gets repetitive due to Wolverine’s limited moveset. Spider-Man had the benefit of variety, through launching enemies into the air and fighting them, or using a wide arsenal of gadgets. This variation is largely absent in Wolverine , where you rely on two move combinations and six special abilities. Pressing the exact same button combination ad nauseam made combat a monotonous slog, especially in the late-game, when enemies soaked up a lot more damage. There are only six special moves — you can equip four at a time — and they take a lot of time to recharge between uses, meaning you’ll press ‘square, square, square, triangle’ (that’s the main combo) and hope that enemies don’t interrupt the animation for the final hit. This could have been fixed in several different ways, I reckon: more button combinations for variation, a faster recharge time for special moves, Wolverine moving on all fours like in Deadpool and Wolverine , or even using a different control scheme. It is literally just these two combos. I recently finished The Blood of Dawnwalker (let us know if you want a review) and found that game’s directional parry and strike system a lot of fun to engage with. Maybe something like that would fit here? The stealth isn’t much fun either; it feels tacked on like an afterthought rather than a key mechanic in the game. Enemies spot you very quickly, and takedown animations are so long that you end up getting spotted anyway. When presented with stealth encounters, I’d opt for open combat because it was less awful. This is emblematic of why Wolverine is a disappointment: there’s a very solid foundation, but Insomniac, playing it safe, have elected against building anything unique or crazy on top of it. Even the boss fights are extremely basic and predictable, designed for the lowest common denominator. I’m with stupid By far, the biggest complaint I have is with the game’s excessive handholding and use of invasive visual cues to guide the player through levels. Sometimes, Logan has to track a character by their scent, which is where this issue is at its most prevalent. As a visual demonstration of his enhanced senses, this is fine. But as I said earlier, these levels are very linear in design, with only one or two paths to go down. I don’t need a permanent blue or red line showing me where to go when there’s only one path. Seriously, Logan even says we need to go through the industrial park. Why is this line here? I have to assume the game was designed with the most casual of casual gamers in mind, but even those players would be able to navigate the levels without the scent trail. Thankfully, these can be turned off, but that only came in with a post-launch patch. It gets worse. There are hidden crates with materials to craft suits in most levels, which you need to find using an audio cue that gets louder when looking in the crate’s direction. Now this is fine, but a giant blue marker reveals the box’s position before the audio cues even kick in, rendering the entire system redundant. Why would I listen for the cue when it’ll be flashed on my screen anyway? At best, this is counter-productive, and at worst, it insults the player’s intelligence. Overall, it’s very frustrating. I hope this sort of thing does not become a pattern in future titles. What a nightmare In terms of side content, Marvel’s Wolverine features Nightmare Doors “hidden” in each of the game’s levels. I use “hidden” in quotes because they’re about as hidden as a billboard on the nearest chaurangi . Giant purple roots sprout out of the ground — accompanied by audio-visual cues and controller vibrations — pointing you to a door that appears out of thin air. Behind these doors lie challenges for the player to complete, which will unlock parts of Wolverine’s memory, and these take the form of combat challenges, traversal time trials and gauntlets. Gauntlets are one of the highlights of the game. These are challenges with up to 25 waves of various enemies that you need to survive. I loved these because, unlike the restrictive story mode, they allow you to get creative with the game’s combat system. Managed to complete all of these except the final wave of the last gauntlet. The campaign didn’t offer enough scenarios to use Wolverine’s abilities against large groups of enemies, but here, there are no restrictions. You face plenty of foes of varying difficulty, allowing you to be more tactical rather than just spamming the square button. The presence of three or four heavy enemies may prompt you to focus on the 15 other smaller ones, for example. Despite my complaints with the combat, I genuinely enjoyed these and looked forward to playing them. They also fit the character perfectly. Just a bit dull, really To sum up, Wolverine is a game that’s been largely declawed. What frustrates me most is that there is a structure for a good game here somewhere ; but Insomniac played it safe and buried it under layers of handholding that leave it boring. There are good moments in the story and the gauntlet challenges rule, but they aren’t enough to justify spending Rs18,000, especially not with other games out now that are (or might be) better. It isn’t even that single-player linear action games have a place in the market — look at 007: First Light — the issue lies in the core of the game’s design: it’s restrictive, doesn’t want to grant player agency and relies on references, flashy visuals and the studio’s prior laurels to keep itself afloat. Given how expensive games are getting, and considering what we’re due to get during the rest of this holiday season, I can’t recommend buying this at full price. If you’re really desperate, get it on sale, or wait for it to come onto the PlayStation Plus Game Catalogue within a year or so. As I said, this is not a bad game. It’s just a very disappointing one. title: Shajar clinches thrilling 100m final as National Athletics Championship starts
description: KARACHI: The flame went from Shajar Abbas’s hands into Ghazala Ramzan’s and then into Arshad Nadeem’s and when Pakistan’s Olympic javelin champion touched it to the cauldron and the fireworks went up over the NED University sports complex on Thursday, the sparse crowd forgot, for a moment, that this was just the 54th National Athletics Championship and not something grander. The cultural dancers came out next, and before long the athletes had wandered off the track and into the performance, trading their blocks and spikes for a few minutes of unchoreographed movement alongside the professionals — competitors and spectators both, turning a modest opening ceremony into something that looked, briefly, like a celebration. Then the flame cooled, the dancing stopped, and the track did what it always does: it turned ceremony back into competition. The men’s 100m went first, and it needed only 10.20 seconds to produce the day’s defining image — Wapda’s Shajar crossing the line a hundredth of a second ahead of 19-year-old Ataullah of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, with Haseeb Ahmed (HEC) a further four-hundredths back in third. It was a photo finish for a title that, on paper, Shajar had no business making close. He holds both the national 100m and 200m records, calls himself simply “Pakistan’s fastest man,” and a little over a year ago was lying in a hospital bed recovering from surgery on a tumour in his shin bone, uncertain whether sprinting again was even realistic. “He [Ataullah] ran pretty good, it got pretty close,” Shajar told Dawn afterwards, with the understatement of a man who knows exactly how much closer it could have gone. “Hopefully we get more competitions like this so the other athletes get more opportunities.” He still feels pain from the injury, he admitted, and his rehabilitation is technically still ongoing — he competed anyway, because competing is the only part of the comeback he can actually control. His next target is the South Asian Games, hosted on Pakistan soil next year. “I will give my best to win a medal for my country on home soil,” he said. For Ataullah, the margin was a lesson rather than a defeat. The Nowshera-born sprinter, fresh off representing Pakistan at this year’s World Athletics U-20 Championship and still the reigning champion of his own age group, spent the race watching the wrong thing. Star javelin thrower Arshad Nadeem lights the torch during the opening ceremony on Thursday.—White Star “I felt he was a bit slow, but when I looked towards him at the end of the race he upped the pace and there I felt he edged me,” Ataullah told Dawn, with the particular clarity of someone replaying the final 20 metres on a loop. He has decided, with the pragmatism of a 19-year-old who has already dominated every junior field put in front of him, that the gap to the seniors is a matter of time rather than talent. “My time will come,” he said. “I have to achieve a lot, hopefully.” Faiqa Riaz, representing Wapda, needed less drama to keep her own crown, winning the women’s 100m in 11.56 seconds, well clear of HEC’s Khoula Omer (12.22) and Iqra Riaz (12.24) of Sindh — though her year has supplied drama enough without the home crowd’s help. She arrived in Karachi having competed at both the Commonwealth Games and the Asian Games in the same year, the latter while fighting food poisoning that hit the day after she landed in Japan. She ran through it anyway, clocking 11.96. “My health deteriorated. I got food poisoning,” she said. “But I played my competition in that condition… so that was also a good time.” Karachi brought its own, smaller complaint — dust in the air, a world away from Faiqa’s training base in Lahore — but she wasn’t about to let the setting dim the result. “We have a National Cham­pionship once a year, so because of that we are very pleased,” she said. Her sights are already on next year’s South Asian Games, and on home advantage doing what Karachi’s dust and Japan’s food poisoning couldn’t. “I’ll try to set a Pakistan record at home and win a gold medal,” she said, before turning the credit over entirely to her corner. “All the responsibility for this achievement is on them, and I would like to dedicate this to them,” she said of coaches Gauhar Shahbaz and Fayyaz Ahmed. “They saved me from injury and brought my peak at the right time.” The opening day also passed without Pakistan Army or Pakistan Railways, with the organising committee confirming both departments were absent. In a statement, it said the Army had “conveyed its readiness and willingness to participate” but that “the necessary departmental approval rema­ined pending,” while Railways “was unable to field an athletics contingent for this year’s championships.” The action kicked off earlier on Thursday with Sindh’s Mahnoor Fatima winning the women’s 5,000m race walk in 32 minutes 32.40 seconds ahead of Wapda’s Ammara Manwar and Punjab’s Savera, while Wapda’s Moham­mad Waqas took the men’s 20,000m walk in 1 hour 50 minutes and 04.1 seconds. HEC’s Khadija Mehreen won the women’s shot put with a throw of 10.85m, and the middle distances went to Wapda’s Nazia Ehsan (women’s 1,500m, 5:09.78) and Sohail Amir (men’s 1,500m, 3:55.40) — four more champions crowned before the lights came up on the complex’s first night. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Growers critcise PTB for failing to purchase surplus tobacco
description: SWABI: The Pakistan Tobacco Board (PTB) has failed to adopt a strategy to purchase surplus tobacco from growers despite the passage of 36 days since the regular buying season ended, it was learnt. Sources in multinational and national companies said that tobacco purchasing was stopped on Sept 15 as the firms had completed their quota for the current year announced by PTB. The sources said PTB’s role in handling tobacco affairs is critical, but its officials always toe the line of companies, leaving the poor growers high and dry. They said it was the responsibility of the Federal Ministry of National Food Security and Research and PTB to devise a strategy binding all national and multinational companies to buy tobacco from farmers in accordance with the rules. However, they said the companies were adopting delaying tactics or were not at all interested in buying the surplus tobacco from growers. Meanwhile, Kashtkar Ittehad Association members said that the surplus tobacco was being purchased at Rs545 per kilogramme compared to over Rs700 per kg during the regular buying period, allowing companies and traders to earn millions at the cost of poor farmers. Iqbal Khan Shewa, the association’s patron-in-chief, told Dawn that both companies and traders exploited the weak financial position of tobacco growers. The sources said the business community and small cigarette manufacturers continued to exploit the prevailing uncertain environment, purchasing tobacco from growers at low prices. They said poor farmers didn’t have any arrangements to store tobacco, forcing them to sell their produce at throwaway rates. Imran Khan, a grower from Maneri Bala region, said: “Officials of the companies and tobacco entrepreneurs are well aware of the fact that the financial position of growers is feeble as they neither have the resources nor arrangements to store the crop.” When contacted, PTB secretary Fakhruddin told Dawn that they would soon start purchasing surplus tobacco from growers. title: Illegal shops, business centres razed in Charsadda, Lakki Marwat
description: CHARSADDA: With anti-encroachment campaigns continuing in different parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, several illegally-built shops, business centres and structures were demolished by authorities on Thursday. In Charsadda, the district administration has launched a large-scale operation against encroachments in line with the instructions of the governor. During the drive, several illegal structures were demolished and encroachments removed in Charsadda city, Peshawar Road, Tangi, Sherpao and other areas. Traders resented the demolition of dozens of shops in Sherpao Bazaar, saying the action against their businesses was taken without prior notice. They called the action illegal and unjust and said it had caused them substantial financial losses and threatened their families’ livelihoods. According to the district administration, the operation aims to reclaim public land, clear roads and markets of encroachers and facilitate movement of pedestrians and traffic. Deputy commissioner Mansoor Arshad said the drive would continue across the district without discrimination. Also, an anti-encroachment operation has been launched in Tangi tehsil under the supervision of assistant commissioner Akhlaq Ahmad and additional assistant commissioner Adan Zahid to reclaim land. A police contingent and municipal staff assisted the administration. Traders complained about the operation in Sherpao Bazaar, claiming that their shops were demolished without prior notice, causing them serious financial issues. Representatives of trader organisations met deputy commissioner Mansoor Arshad and conveyed their grievances to them. The DC promised effective resolution of their issues. In Lakki Marwat, several temporary and permanent structures were pulled down during the operation on Thursday. Deputy commissioner Shahid Rafiq Gandapur led the operation wherein anti-encroachment squad of the tehsil municipal administration removed illegal buildings and structures from both sides of the busy Peshawar-Karachi Highway in the Serai Gambila Bazaar. Heavy machinery, including excavators and tractors, were used in the operation. Assistant commissioner Gohar Ali Khan, TMO Almar Khan and other relevant officials were also present. During the operation, both sides of the Indus Highway were cleared from encroachments. DC Gandapur said that the administration would not allow anyone to occupy state-owned land or roadsides for commercial or other purposes. He said that every inch of the government land would be protected and those involved in erecting illegal encroachments would face stern legal action. The DC said that using roadsides for business activities or displaying goods by traders hindered the smooth flow of traffic and that his administration would not tolerate any illegal activity. The anti-encroachment actions were also carried out in Maradan, Nowshera and Bajaur districts on Thursday. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Directorates of erstwhile Fata placed under ADS control
description: PESHAWAR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi has approved the transfer of administrative control of directorates and other major institutions in the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Fata) to the newly-established Area Development Secretariat (ADS), almost doing away with the arrangements put in place after the merger of tribal areas with the province in 2018. The ADS has also notified the establishment of the office of chief police officer for the designated districts. The ADS, established following the imposition of an emergency in the province on Oct 11, has been tasked with managing 12 designated districts. “The directorates and major institutions of erstwhile Fata, which were placed under the administrative supervision and control of the respective departments of the government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa through notifications issued by the erstwhile Establishment Department during the period from October 24, 2018, to March 27, 2019, as detailed in the schedule annexed to this notification, shall henceforth stand placed under the administrative supervision and control of the Area Development Secretariat (ADS), headed by the Additional Chief Secretary/Administrator (Designated Districts),” a notification issued by the human resource management department said. Office of chief police officer for 12 designated districts notified It said the administrative control and reporting arrangements prescribed through the earlier notifications would accordingly be modified, with the directorates and institutions listed in the schedule reporting to the respective ADS secretaries, as determined by the additional chief secretary for the designated districts, instead of the corresponding departments. The notification said the transfer of administrative control would include the functions, responsibilities, records, assets, equipment, office facilities and other resources pertaining to the directorates and institutions in the designated districts. “Their existing sanctioned posts, budgetary provisions and other administrative arrangements shall be appropriately identified and adjusted in consultation with the concerned departments, subject to applicable laws, rules and orders, ensuring continuity of their functions and public service delivery,” it said. The directorates and institutions placed under the ADS include those responsible for education, Zakat and Ushr, social welfare, population welfare, agriculture extension, livestock and dairy development, fisheries, forests, irrigation, sports, industries, technical education, minerals, oil and gas, director general projects, Fata, agriculture research, local government, works and services and public health engineering. Also, the Fata planning and development department, information directorate, law and order department, Levies Training Centre in Shakass and Fata Disaster Management Authority have been placed under the ADS. Through a separate notification, the human resource management department temporarily transferred 30 posts in grades 17-20, along with their supporting ministerial and other staff, from the respective KP government departments to the ADS. The positions include five special secretaries in BS-20, 10 deputy secretaries in BS-18 and 15 section officers in BS-17. “The incumbents of the five posts of special secretaries (BS-20) shall be designated as secretaries to government, ADS, and shall exercise the powers and perform the functions of secretaries to government in respect of the business assigned to them by the ACS designated districts,” the notification said. It said the officers designated as ADS secretaries would use ministerial suites Nos. 12, 13, 14 and 15 in the Ministers’ Block at the Civil Secretariat in Peshawar, which had already been made available for the purpose, along with associated office facilities. Deputy secretaries in BS-18 and section officers in BS-17 posted to the ADS will continue working from their existing offices, using the furniture, equipment, supporting staff and other facilities currently available to them, until further orders. The notification said the officers posted to the ADS would also be allowed to retain and use the government vehicles already provided to them, along with associated facilities, until further orders. On Wednesday, the ADS notified the names of five officials whose services the human resource management department had placed at its disposal as secretaries for the newly designated region. title: Woman dies, four others hurt in Shangla landslide
description: SHANGLA: A woman died and four others were injured when a landslide buried them while they were digging clay for domestic use in Shangla district on Thursday. According to local residents, the incident occurred in the Kuza Awarai area, where five women had gone to collect clay for making traditional stoves and other household items. A portion of the earth suddenly collapsed, burying them underneath. Local residents rushed to the scene and launched a rescue effort. After strenuous efforts, all five women were pulled from the debris and shifted to the Tehsil Headquarters Hospital in Puran for treatment. One of the injured women succumbed to her injuries at the hospital, while the remaining four received medical treatment. The condition of one of the injured women was stated to be critical, prompting doctors to refer her to Swat for further treatment. The deceased woman’s body was handed over to her heirs after completion of the medico-legal formalities. In a separate incident, a tractor driver was killed when his vehicle plunged into a ravine in the Navy Kaly area of Puran tehsil on Thursday. According to police, the tractor was on its way along a rough village road when it plunged into the ravine, killing the driver, identified as Ziaur Rehman. Police said the body was shifted to the Tehsil Headquarters Hospital in Puran, where doctors pronounced him dead. It was later handed over to his heirs after the necessary formalities. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Utilities in Rawalpindi barred from digging up roads without permission
description: Labourers dig Raja Zafarul Haq Road for laying new gas pipeline at Mohalla Dhok Hukamdad, in Rawalpindi on Thursday. — Online RAWALPINDI: The divisional administration on Thursday told utility services departments that no agency would commence development work without road-cutting permission and a no-objection certificate (NOC). Commissioner Rawalpindi Salman Ghani issued the directive at a meeting held to review road-cutting permissions and the installation and management of underground utility lines by various government departments. He said that repeated road cutting in urban areas caused inconvenience to the public, created traffic congestion besides causing wastage of public resources. He said all concerned departments must ensure comprehensive planning and effective coordination before undertaking any road-cutting activity. The commissioner directed that all departments, organisations and service providers requiring road cutting for the installation, relocation or repair of their services must be brought on board through a coordinated mechanism. “All relevant departments must share timely information regarding their upcoming projects and underground utility lines to avoid the need to excavate newly constructed roads,” he said. He stressed that road cutting must remain the last resort. Wherever feasible, modern alternative techniques, including thrust boring and ducting, should be adopted to minimise damage to road surfaces and infrastructure. Mr Ghani further directed that whenever road cutting is permitted under unavoidable circumstances, the affected road must be restored to its original standard and strength. All restoration work, including refilling and reconstruction, must be completed within 15 days of road cutting, he said. During the meeting, PTCL’s request for an NOC for work in Shah Khalid Colony Phase II was approved, with a deadline of two days for completion. Similarly, Wasa was granted permission to lay a 12-inch-diameter sewer line at Al-Khidmat Al-Razi Children’s Hospital. The commissioner directed that the work must be completed within seven days under all circumstances, with an alternative traffic route provided during construction. A request for an NOC to reactivate the colony’s sewerage line on Mushtaq Baig Shaheed Road was also considered, with a two-day completion timeline stipulated. SNGPL was granted permission to carry out work in 10 localities, including Pirwadhai, Novelty Cinema, Khurshid Cinema, Chhajji Mohalla, Asghar Mall, Fazalabad, Dhoke Hukamdad, Dhoke Kala Khan and Chandni Chowk. Mr Ghani added that utility shifting and road-cutting requirements must be incorporated into the initial planning stages of all major development projects. He directed that joint meetings of all concerned departments be held before the commencement of any project to ensure proper coordination and prevent roads from being excavated again after project completion. title: Proposed amendments to Islamabad LG law cast doubt on Dec 20 polls
description: ISLAMABAD: A day after the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) announced the schedule for local government elections in Islamabad on December 20, the National Assembly Standing Committee on Interior presented a report to the lower house seeking amendments to the Islamabad Capital Territory Local Government Act, 2015, casting doubt on the already announced election schedule. The report on the Islamabad Capital Territory Local Government (Amendment) Bill, 2026 (Ordinance No. II of 2026), was presented by committee chairman Raja Khurram Shahzad Nawaz of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) during Thursday’s session of the National Assembly. The bill proposes major changes, including dividing Islamabad into three town corporations, each headed by a separate mayor and deputy mayors. The government introduced the bill in March this year, but the committee’s report was presented a day after the ECP announced the election schedule. NA committee report proposes three town corporations, separate mayors and greater powers for administrators Interestingly, Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) members of the committee, including MNAs Abdul Qadir Patel, Syed Rafiullah, Sardar Nabeel Ahmed Gabol and Nawabzada Mir Jamal Khan Raisani, along with Pashtunkhwa National Awami Party’s Khushal Khan Kakar, submitted dissenting notes on the bill. Under the proposed legislation, Islamabad would have three town corporations, while union councils would be delimited on the basis of population equality, taking into account the latest official census and administrative convenience. A town corporation would comprise a mayor and two deputy mayors, the chairmen of all union councils within its jurisdiction as general members, four women members, one peasant or worker, one trader or businessman, one youth member and one non-Muslim member. The bill also proposes expanding the powers of administrators, including authorising them to impose taxes. It seeks to remove the existing six-month limit on an administrator’s tenure. The statement of objects and reasons accompanying the bill says the ICT Local Government Act, 2015, was enacted to establish an elected local government system and devolve political, administrative and financial authority to elected representatives to promote good governance, effective service delivery and transparent decision-making through public participation at the grassroots level. It states that amendments are necessary to ensure that the benefits of the law reach the grassroots level. Amendments have been proposed to Sections 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16, 29, 63, 88 and 93 of the existing law. The proposed changes would replace the Metropolitan Corporation with three town corporations. An amendment to Section 29 would also allow the government to appoint an administrator to exercise the powers and perform the functions of a local government after its term expires. On Wednesday, the ECP announced another schedule for local government elections in the capital, fixing December 20 as polling day. The term of Islamabad’s local government expired in February 2021, and the ECP was required to hold elections within 120 days. However, the federal government and the commission have repeatedly undertaken delimitation exercises and announced election schedules before postponing the polls. Constituencies and union councils have been delimited six times, while the election schedule has been issued four times. The previous programme, announced on October 9, had fixed polling for February 2026. The federal government continued to postpone elections, citing various reasons, including proposed amendments to the Local Government Act, depriving around 2.5 million Islamabad residents of an elected local government system. Whenever an election schedule was announced, the local chapter of the opposition Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) reportedly claimed that the government, fearing defeat, would find a way to avoid holding the polls. The ruling PML-N’s local chapter consistently rejected the allegations, maintaining that the government wanted an effective and vibrant local government system in Islamabad. title: Delayed filing of ownership statements: Lahore High Court annuls SECP penalties on mill directors
description: LAHORE: The Lahore High Court has annulled penalties imposed by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) on the directors of a weaving mill for a delayed filing of beneficial ownership statements. Justice Jawad Hassan allowed seven connected commercial appeals, including the one by Fawad Ahmed Mukhtar, the company’s chairman and also the head of the Fatima Group. The SECP had fined each director Rs60,000 under the Securities Act, 2015, for a 253-day delay in filing Form 5 after their re-appointment. Section 103 of the Act, read with Regulation 3(4) of the 2015 Regulations, requires directors of listed companies to file the form within seven days. The appellate bench of the SECP later halved the penalty to Rs30,000 each and the SECP issued a recovery notice to the appellants. The directors argued that the delay was inadvertent and caused by the Covid-19 disruptions and administrative difficulties. They said their re-appointment involved no change in shareholding, beneficial ownership or position. They also noted that the forms were filed on Dec 31, 2021, after an SECP letter of Dec 23 but before any show-cause notice was issued. The SECP’s special prosecutor objected to the maintainability of the appeals and stressed that disclosure rules protect investors and market confidence. However, the judge rejected the objection. Justice Hassan acknowledged that the reporting requirement is mandatory and cannot be treated as optional, even for family-owned companies. He observed, however, that the disclosure regime aims at actual disclosure of relevant interests rather than formal filing alone. He noted the forms were filed before adjudication began and the SECP itself had accepted there was no concealment or misrepresentation, therefore, the regulatory purpose had in substance been achieved. The judge also noted that an SECP clarification of April 20, 2022, indicated ambiguity over whether Form 5 applied to re-appointment of the same directors. He held that reducing the penalty did not answer the question of whether any penalty was justified. The judge referred to the principles for regulators dealing with listed companies, including proportionate penalties, due process, protection against arbitrary enforcement and effective judicial review. He ruled that disproportionate sanctions can damage shareholder value and market confidence. The judge allowed the appeals and set aside the orders of the SECP and its appellate bench. title: UNIDO to mobilise $40m for Sindh rural development, climate-resilient projects
description: KARACHI: The Sindh government and the United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO) on Thursday agreed to deepen cooperation for inclusive rural development, climate-resilient infrastructure and employment generation, with UNIDO planning to mobilise around $40 million for a dedicated programme for the province. The understanding was reached at a meeting between Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah and UNIDO Deputy Director General and Managing Director Ms Fatou Haidara at the CM House. According to a press statement issued by the CM House, the commitment includes mobilising around $40 million from international donors and investors for a dedicated five-year development programme for Sindh under UNIDO’s Programme for Country Partnership (PCP) 2025-2030 aimed at inclusive economic growth, climate-resilient infrastructure and employment generation. Ms Haidara informed the chief minister that Pakistan had already signed the PCP framework with the UNIDO and that the organisation now intended to formulate a Sindh-specific programme based on the province’s development needs and priorities. The chief minister welcomed the initiative and said that the provincial government was ready to pursue it in coordination with the climate change ministry and other relevant federal stakeholders and to seek its endorsement as a priority development programme. The meeting, attended among others by Labour Minister Saeed Ghani, Planning & Development Minister Jam Khan Shoro, Special Assistant to CM on Investment Syed Qasim Naveed and P&D Chairman Najam Shah, also reviewed progress under the European Union-funded Poverty Alleviation and Inclusive Development Across Rural Sindh (PAIDAR) programme. The UNIDO delegation included Asia-Pacific Region Chief Jie Zhao, Officer-in-Charge Badar-ul-Islam and National Technical Advisor for PAIDAR Farooque Ahmed Siddiqui. Minister Shoro told the meeting that PAIDAR, being implemented by UNIDO with a €49.55 million EU grant, was working across Thatta, Sujawal, Badin, Thar­parkar and Larkana districts to reduce poverty, strengthen local economies, improve public services and create employ­ment opportunities for women and youth. The programme combines investment in rural infrastructure and community facilities with financial grants for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), technical assistance and institutional capacity-building. The chief minister appreciated PAIDAR’s contribution to rebuilding flood-affected communities through climate-resilient settlement planning in collaboration with the Sindh People’s Housing for Flood Affectees (SPHF). Special Assistant Qasim Naveed cited examples of beneficiaries who had converted financial assistance into viable businesses, including a woman entrepreneur who opened a restaurant in Badin and an entrepreneur in Larkana who set up a pasta-making facility linked to a flour mill. The meeting was informed that Community Resilient Settlement Development Plans (CRSDPs) had been prepared for around 300 villages across the five PAIDAR districts, laying the foundation for climate-informed planning and resilient infrastructure. It was informed that following the development of a model village at Lakho Bhambhro in Thatta in collaboration with the SPHF, the UNIDO was supporting the expansion of the approach to an additional 100 villages. The initiative integrates safe drinking water, sanitation, drainage, roads and energy-efficient facilities to enhance living conditions and strengthen resilience to climate risks. The programme is also supporting Rural Growth Centres (RGCs) to improve access to public services and boost local economic activity. The meeting was informed that PAIDAR would support skills development for 200 young people from the five target districts through reputable training institutions. The nine-to-12-month programmes will focus on emerging and market-oriented trades, including hospitality, electric vehicles, solar technologies and other sectors with strong employment and entrepreneurship potential. The meeting also reviewed UNIDO’s technical assistance for the Sindh Development Portfolio Management System (SDPMS), being implemented with the Planning and Development Department to modernise management of the provincial development portfolio. The model village initiative integrates essential community infrastructure, including safe drinking water, sanitation, drainage, roads, energy-efficient facilities, and other improvements designed to enhance living conditions and strengthen resilience to climate-related risks. The programme is also supporting the development of Rural Growth Centres (RGCs) to improve access to public services, strengthen local economic activity, and create opportunities for enterprise development. The chief minister appreciated the integrated approach and stressed the importance of ensuring that community infrastructure and livelihood initiatives deliver lasting benefits to rural populations. title: Couple shot dead in coach near Sukkur; two held
description: SUKKUR: A couple who had contracted a free-will marriage were shot dead in a passenger coach on the National Highway near the VIG Gate, within the limits of the Baiji Sharif police station in Panu Aqil, Sukkur district, on Thursday evening. The victims were reportedly travelling to Karachi when the attack took place. Police said armed assailants opened fire on the couple and tried to flee. The victims were identified as Sidra Samejo and Deedar Sheikh. Their bodies were taken to a nearby hospital for a post-mortem examination. Police described the killings as being committed in the name of honour. They said further investigation was under way to establish the circumstances. A free-will affidavit dated Sept 28, 2026, identifies a woman named Sidra, daughter of Abdul Hakeem Samejo, and gives details of her previous marriage to a man named Abdul Hanan. According to the document, she has four children from that marriage. She alleged that her former husband mistreated her and pronounced talaq three times on Sept 11, 2024, in the presence of witnesses, after which she lived at her parents’ home. It records that she entered into a nikah with Deedar Ali, son of Muhammad Ishaque Shaikh, on April 25, 2026. title: Constituencies ‘re-described’ in KP sans mandatory public hearing
description: ISLAMABAD: In yet another controversial move, the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) has partially revised the description of several constituencies of national and provincial assemblies in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa without inviting any objections required under the law. A notification issued by the ECP says the move follows administrative changes in revenue units between April 2, 2024 and Jan 27, 2026 and cites Rule 15 of the Election Rules 2017 to justify the move to ‘partially modify’ a notification issued around three years ago, on Nov 30, 2023. Section 15 of the Election Rules states: “The Commission may re-describe a constituency in case of any change in administrative units; however, in doing so, the limit of the constituency shall remain the same.” Section 22 (1) of the Elections Act 2017, which deals with the power of commission to make amendment, alteration or modification in the final list of constituencies, reads: “Notwithstanding anything contained in this act, the commission may, at any time but at least four months before notification of the election programme, of its own motion and for reasons to be recorded, make such amendments, alterations or modifications in the final list of constituencies published under sub-section (4) of section 21 or in the areas included in a constituency, as it deems necessary”. Section 22(2) says the commission shall publish in the official gazette and on its website the proposed amendments, alterations or modifications with their justifications and invite and hear representations in respect thereof before taking final decision thereon. According to the notification, three Swat seats have been re-aligned after creation of Bar Swat District vide notification dated Jan 27, 2026. NA-2 now comprises Bah­rain tehsil, Khwaz­a­k­hela tehsil and part of Cha­rbagh. NA-3 covers Ming­ora/Bab­uzai area, including six patwar circles of Babuzai as described, Barikot tehsil and selected patwar circles of Kabal tehsil. NA-4 covers Matta tehsil of Bar Swat district and remaining patwar circles of Kabal tehsil of Swat district. NA-36 Hangu-cum-Orakzai-cum-Karak now comprises re-constituted Hangu district, Orakzai district, and two villages/mouzas — Darshi and Matho Khel — of Patwar Circle Mardan Khel, Qanungo Halqa Banda Daud Shah, Banda Daud Shah tehsil of Karak district. In effect, Darshi and Matho Khel villages have been added to this constituency from Karak. NA-38 Karak now comprises Karak district re-co­nstituted vide April 2, 2024 notification, excluding the two villages of Darshi and Matho Khel of Banda Daud Shah tehsil, which have been shifted to NA-36. NA-43 Tank-cum-Dera Ismail Khan-cum-Paha­rpur now comprises Tank district, Kulachi and Daraband tehsils plus Darazinda Sub-Division, excluding Koh-i-Bahara of Dera Ismail Khan district, and Paniala tehsil and part of Paharpur tehsil of newly created Paharpur district. NA-44 Dera Ismail Khan-cum-Paharpur now comprises Yarik, Shorkot Qan­ungo Halqas, Chahkan Qanungo Halqa, excluding Hassani and Shero Khona, Muryali Qanungo Halqa, excluding Muryali, Shero Nau, Mapal, Fatah, Kotla Habib, and Ratta Kulachi Patwar Circle of Dera Ismail Khan tehsil of Dera Ismail Khan district, and Band Kurai Qanungo Halqa of Paharpur tehsil of Paharpur district newly created vide notification dated Nov 26, 2025. NA-45 Dera Ismail Khan now comprises Census Cha­rge No. 5 Dera Ismail Khan MC, Census Charge No. 1 Dera Ismail Khan Cantonment, Dera Ismail Khan Qanungo Halqa, exc­luding Ratta Kulachi, Mur­yali Patwar Circle, Parowa tehsil and Fatah Patwar Circle of Muryali, Koh-i-Bahara of Darazinda Sub-Div­i­sion, Hassani and She­ro Khona of Chahkan Qanu­ngo Halqa and Shero Nau, Mapal and Kotla Habib of Muryali Qanungo Halqa. In broad terms, NA-44 has been made Dera city plus cantonment plus Shorkot area plus Band Kurai of Paharpur, while NA-45 covers Parowa, Dar­aband, Darazinda, Kulachi, Paha­rpur and Muryali areas as per new district limits. title: Seven suspects gunned down in Karachi ‘encounters’
description: KARACHI: Seven suspected criminals were shot dead in alleged police encounters in the city on Thursday. According to officials at the Taimuria police station, a team of the Shaheen Force signaled two riders of a motorcycle to stop for checking near the DC Office in North Nazimabad, but they opened fire and tried to speed away. They were chased along the road running parallel to the DC office, the police said, adding that in the ensuing encounter, both the suspects were shot dead. title: Labour federations oppose Pakistan Mineral Development Corporation's privatisation

title: Balochistan Assembly defers move to abolish Sardari system
description: QUETTA: A resolution seeking the abolition of the Sardari system in Balochistan, moved by Jamaat-i-Islami MPA Maulana Hidayatur Rehman Baloch, could not be taken up by the provincial assembly on Thursday as the house deferred its entire agenda following the death of former provincial education minister Sardar Nisar Ali Hazara. Deputy Speaker Ghazala Gola, who presided over the sitting, announced that, in recognition of the late lawmaker’s services to the province, the assembly would adopt a condolence resolution and defer all other business until the next sitting. Sardar Nisar Ali Hazara passed away in Quetta on Oct 20. A large number of people, including prominent Hazara community leaders, political figures and others, attended his funeral prayers. The deputy speaker said that, in accordance with parliamentary tradition, the sitting would be limited to a prayer and a condolence resolution in honour of the deceased, while the remaining agenda would be taken up at the next sitting. Adopts resolution paying tribute to late education minister Maulana Hidayatur Rehman Baloch moved a motion seeking the postponement of the assembly’s proceedings until Monday, Oct 26, in recognition of the late former MPA’s services. The house approved the motion, following which the deputy speaker announced that the remaining agenda would be deferred until the next sitting at 3pm on Monday. Presenting the condolence resolution, Mr Baloch said the house expressed deep grief and sorrow over the death of Sardar Nisar Ali Hazara, a former member of the Balochistan Assembly, who passed away on Oct 20. Mr Hazara was elected to the Balochistan Assembly from constituency PB-2, Quetta, in the 1997 general elections and subsequently served as provincial education minister. The resolution paid tribute to his valuable services to the province, stating that his death had deprived Balochistan of a hardworking and capable politician. It also extended heartfelt condolences to his family and prayed that Almighty Allah grant the deceased a high place in heaven and give patience to the bereaved family. The house unanimously adopted the resolution, after which the deputy speaker adjourned the sitting until 3pm on Monday. The resolution seeking the abolition of the Sardari system is now expected to be taken up on Oct 26. It may be recalled that a resolution calling for the abolition of the Sardari system was first moved in the Balochistan Provincial Assembly on June 8, 1972, when Sardar Ataullah Mengal was chief minister of the province’s first coalition government, formed by the National Awami Party (NAP) and the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam (JUI). Fazila Aaliyani, a female member of the NAP, moved the resolution, which called for the eradication of what it described as exploitative and outdated institutions, particularly the Sardari, jirga and tribal systems, to promote social and economic progress in the province. Since the provincial assembly lacked the constitutional authority to abolish the system directly, the resolution called on the federal government to take legislative action. The federal government subsequently enacted the System of Sardari (Abolition) Act, 1976, during the tenure of former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. Mr Bhutto had announced the abolition of the Sardari system in Balochistan while addressing a public meeting at Quetta’s Liaquat Park in April 1976. The then governor of Balochistan, Khan of Kalat Mir Ahmed Yar Khan, was also present. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Russia, Ukraine trade attacks after US envoy meets Putin
description: • Witkoff briefs Russian president on ‘new aspects in approaches of Europeans and Kyiv’ from Oslo meeting • Moscow mayor says 630 drones launched towards region • Russian strikes injure 15 people in Kyiv • Kremlin aide tells media Russia ready to resume trilateral talks in mid-November KYIV: Russia and Ukraine traded major attacks overnight, with Moscow’s mayor saying on Thursday that 630 drones had been launched towards the region, shortly after a US envoy held talks with the Russian president in Saint Petersburg. It was “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war, US President Donald Trump said after his envoy Steve Witkoff’s meeting with Vladimir Putin on Wednesday. The Kremlin indicated it was “in principle” open to the resumption of trilateral talks between the two sides with the United States. But attacks did not let up in the wake of the visit, with Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko posting on social media that strikes had wounded 15 people in the Ukrainian capital, eight of whom needed hospitalisation. He said in a separate post that strikes had damaged metro infrastructure at the Pivdenny Bridge, which officials said had restricted traffic between parts of the city. Ukraine’s airforce posted a war­ning in the early hours of “more ballistic missiles towards Kyiv” and ins­tructed residents to stay in shelters. Moscow’s mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that two people had been wounded during mostly-intercepted barrages of 630 drones headed towards the region, 163 of which were approaching the capital city. Witkoff had flown to Russia from a meeting with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, which was aimed at smoothing over a bitter rift between Trump and the Ukrainian leader. Witkoff praised Putin as a “humanitarian” for freeing US citizen Stephen Hubbard, but the Kremlin warned after the meeting that while Moscow was “in principle” willing to restart talks there was little “substance” in Ukrainian and European peace proposals the US diplomat had delivered. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters that Russia was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral talks in mid-November — after the US midterm elections — and that the Kremlin wanted them to focus on post-war security. ‘Work left to do’ Ushakov said Witkoff brie­fed Putin on “some new asp­ects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv” from the Oslo meeting, adding though that “there wasn’t really much substance in them”. A summit between Putin, Trump and China’s Xi Jinping was also being prepared in China’s Shenzhen for next month, Ushakov said, calling it “the first such meeting in history”. During their three-hour meeting, Witkoff praised Putin for granting Trump’s request to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a “mercenary” fighting for Ukraine. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian — you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff said.
