title: Israeli fire kills four in Gaza, Syrian man
description: CAIRO/JAKARTA: Israeli strikes and gunfire killed at least four people in the Gaza Strip in separate incidents on Thursday, health officials in the enclave said. In Gaza City, a strike on a car killed at least one person, medics said. They earlier said there had been two deaths. A crowd gathered around the burning wreckage, as orange-vested emergency crews sprayed it with water, photos from the scene showed. Other strikes killed a Palestinian man on a bike in the southern city of Khan Yunis and a man near Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, and gunfire killed a woman near the Jabalia refugee camp, in the north, the medics added. Israel’s military said it had struck Hamas in Khan Yunis, Nuseirat and Gaza City, but that it was not aware of the reported incident in Jabalia. Israel has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks. Francesca Albanese urges Indonesia to reconsider involvement in Trump’s Gaza board Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace deal. Last year’s US-brokered ceasefire calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops. Israeli airstrikes have continued. At least 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire, according to the territory’s health officials, while Israel says four soldiers have been killed. Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza. Syrian man killed Separately, a Syrian man with a disability was killed on Thursday by Israeli fire during an incursion in the country’s south where Israel has stepped up operations. The Israeli military has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria and conducted frequent incursions into its territory since new authorities toppled longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. “A civilian with a disability was killed on Thursday by fire from the Israeli occupation forces during their incursion into the village of Jamla” in Daraa province, Syrian state news agency SANA reported. Israeli forces entered a neighbourhood and placed snipers on the rooftops after bombing the area late on Wednesday, the report said. Syria condemned “in the strongest terms the Israeli occupation forces’ crime”, a foreign ministry statement said, adding that “targeting civilians is a grave violation” of international law. Trump’s Gaza board Indonesia should reconsider its involvement in US President Donald Trump’s Gaza peace plan because it is being shaped by Israel and the US and lacks a Palestinian voice, the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories said on Thursday. Trump announced in January that he was setting up a “Board of Peace” to address global conflicts typically handled by the UN. Indonesia, the world’s largest Muslim-majority nation, has said it would be a member of the new body and it has also pledged troops to be deployed to Gaza as part of an international stabilisation force. Francesca Albanese, a human rights lawyer and UN special rapporteur known for her criticism of Israel, said in an interview in Jakarta that Indonesia has historically supported the Palestinian cause but joining the board was dangerous. Indonesia’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that its Board of Peace discussions remained on hold, reiterating its earlier position. A number of Western capitals have criticised Albanese, while the US has imposed sanctions on her. “I understand [Indonesia’s] good intentions. I still think that it’s very dangerous, because it risks to normalise a very abnormal mechanism,” she said. Albanese said that, legally, Israel could not have a role in determining the future of Palestinians. Rights experts have criticised Trump’s board for not including a Palestinian representative, though it is meant to supervise the temporary governance of a Palestinian territory. A board official rejected the suggestion that the Palestinians had been excluded, however, saying: “Palestinian leadership and ownership remain central to the process.” The official said Gaza’s civilian administration and recovery efforts are led by the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, which is made up of Palestinian professionals from Gaza and led by former Palestinian Authority official Ali Shaath. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: UN fund moves to provide $20m aid for Nepal
description: WASHINGTON: The United Nations’ climate loss and damage fund moved on Thursday to provide $20 million in aid sought by flood-stricken Nepal, the first time it has set aside money for any country, in a key test of the body’s credibility. In an extraordinary meeting, the fund’s board agreed to earmark the modest sum for the Himalayan country, which was hit in August by tsunami-like floods triggered by a climate-induced ice and rock avalanche that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing. Camila Minerva Rodriguez Tavarez, the Dominican co-chair of the board, called the outcome  “truly historic” and thanked members for  “allowing us to act promptly and have a response to Nepal.” Reacting to the news, Nepal’s finance minister Swarnim Wagle said:  “The fact that they could convene this emergency meeting in response to our letter and commit $20 million of grant money is very welcome.” The decision does not, however, mean that Nepal will immediately receive the funding, which amounts to less than 0.5 percent of the government’s $4.78 billion estimate for reconstruction. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: International Criminal Court wins EU’s Sakharov prize
description: STRASBOURG: Facing US sanctions, the International Criminal Court was on Thursday awarded the European Union’s top rights prize, in a show of support that risks upsetting President Donald Trump. “The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” said European Parliament chief Roberta Metsola in announcing the award. The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize “at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges”. “Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said. This month, the United States announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. Trump’s administration has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick”, furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza. The win comes after ex-ICC judge Navi Pillay, who also served as UN rights chief, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this month — a choice Trump slammed as “disgraceful”, arguing the award should have gone to him. The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the US sanctions — which will come into force in six months — and has said it is “ready to take any necessary measures” to make sure the court can keep working. “The International Criminal Court must be free to pursue its mission, independently, and without pressure or intimidation,” EU chief Ursula von der Leyen posted online after the prize was announced. Brussels is hoping to use the delay before the sanctions are applied to try to talk the US down, but is also eyeing implementing a “blocking statute” to shield the ICC from Washington. Three finalists Set up in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organisations to recognise their fight for human rights or democracy. The ICC was among three finalists this year, alongside Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, representing those prosecuted by the Iranian government. The nominees are put forward by the political groupings in the EU and the winner is chosen by senior lawmakers. An award ceremony will be held in December. Lissu, head of Tanzania’s opposition Chadema party, was detained in April 2025. He faces a possible death penalty if convicted of treason for allegedly inciting the public to boycott elections last year. Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 21, have respectively been sentenced to death and 36 years in prison for having taken part in anti-government protests in Iran. Other recent high-profile winners of the Sakharov prize have been Venezuelan opposition chief Maria Corina Machado, deceased Russian Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny and the people of Ukraine. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Thousands protest in Poland for abortion rights
description: WARSAW: Thousands protested in Warsaw and over 20 other Polish cities on Thursday seeking abortion rights on the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban imposed by Poland’s highest court. The demonstrations came days after parliament passed two bills that would ease abortion restrictions in the Catholic country, which are likely to be vetoed by Poland’s conservative president. “These are breadcrumbs,” Kinga Jelinska, director of the Women Help Women Foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, said. In the capital Warsaw, about 1,000 protestors demonstrated in front of parliament despite rain. “Over the last six years, nothing has really changed,” said 36 year-old Milia Niemiec, who manages the  “Abotak” abortion centre, which provides women with access to resources, including pills, and a space to be able to seek support or carry out the pharmacological abortion. Currently, abortion is only legal in Poland when a pregnancy results from a criminal act, like rape or incest, or when it threatens the life or health of the mother. Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government promised to liberalise abortion laws ahead of its 2023 election victory, but divisions within the coalition have slowed progress. “We demand decriminalisation and access to abortion through the public healthcare system,” the protest organisers, which include several Polish activist and advocacy groups, wrote in an Instagram post. One bill would partially decriminalise the termination of a pregnancy and decriminalise assisting abortion — which is currently punishable by up to three years in prison, while the second would reverse the effects of a 2020 ruling by Poland’s highest court, the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which outlawed abortion in cases of severe foetal deformities. Before the ruling, 98 percent of legal abortions in Poland were performed for this reason. According to data from Poland’s National Health Fund (NFZ), only 573 abortions took place in Polish public hospitals in the first half of 2026. Last year, public hospitals carried out 851 abortions, according to the NFZ. The restrictions in 2020 set off a torrent of protests which became the largest demonstrations in Poland since the 1989 anti-communist movement. President Karol Nawrocki, who was endorsed by the then ruling Law and Justice (PiS) party that championed and upheld the 2020 court ruling, is expected to veto both bills. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Trump ordered to sit for deposition in his $10bn BBC lawsuit
description: WASHINGTON: A federal judge on Thursday ordered Donald Trump to sit for a deposition by December 11 in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC , which has accused the US president of stalling to avoid answering questions under oath, the Associated Press reported. Trump is suing Britain’s publicly funded broadcaster for at least $10 billion over a misleadingly edited clip of a speech. The case is one of several Trump has privately filed against the news media as part of a wider pressure campaign against coverage he dislikes. US Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett ordered Trump to take questions from the BBC ’s lawyers under oath in a ruling from the bench at a court hearing on Thursday, according to the AP . Trump cancelled a deposition in October, citing conflicts with his presidential duties. Trump’s lawsuit filed in December in Florida federal court accuses the BBC of intentionally misleading viewers into thinking he directed supporters to storm the US Capitol by splicing together different parts of a January 6, 2021 speech. The BBC admitted the edits were misleading and apologised to Trump, though it denies being liable for defamation. In court filings, the broadcaster has accused Trump and his lawyers of dragging their feet in response to their requests for records and other information that is exch­anged between parties in a process known as discovery. The BBC is seeking financial records from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club and the web of business entities associated with him, saying the information is necessary to defend against Trump’s damages claims. Trump’s lawyers say the requests are too broad and irrelevant to the case. They have also denied in court filings that Trump is avoiding a deposition, saying Trump’s duties and security needs must take precedence. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Nearly all coral reefs risk collapse in 50 years: IUCN
description: YEREVAN: Nearly all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075 due to climate change, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on Thursday. In the first global assessment of its kind, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96 percent of the planet’s coral reef systems as  “critically endangered” — its highest risk category. Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change, which is warming the world’s oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events. “The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems,” said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment. The emergence this year of a  “super” El Nino, the natural warming phenomenon, also presents a risk to corals, Gudka said at a news conference at the UN’s COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia. The IUCN presented its findings at COP17, where governments are under pressure to make progress on a landmark pact to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. For its assessment, the IUCN used the  “middle-of-the-road” scenario from the UN’s panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7C above pre-industrial levels by 2100. The world is on track for 2.6C warming this century under current global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions, the United Nations warned on Wednesday. “Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat dri­­­­ving coral reef decline worldwide,” the IUCN said in a statement. Overfishing is also hurting corals as certain herbivores and predators he­­­­lp control algae and maintain an ecological balance, the organisation said. The overexploitation of parrotfish and other groupers threatens 63pc of coral reef ecosystems. Coastal development, pollution, tourism and more frequent storms are among other threats. Critically endangered coral The IUCN’s analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 square kilometres. The world’s largest and most biodiverse coral reefs are among those classified as critically endangered — Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in southeast Asia and the western Pacific, the Caribbean’s Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System, and the Red Sea coral reefs. A reef ecosystem collapses when hard corals — which build its living foundation — largely disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges. A study published in the journal Nature last week found that, by 2020, nearly half of coral species were at  “elevated relative risk of extinction”, with climate change the main driver of this decline. Despite its warning, the IUCN said coral reefs in most parts of the world  “are not yet lost”. If scientists look only at what has happened over the past 50 years, excluding future climate projections, 24 percent of coral reef ecosystems would be deemed critically endangered instead of 96pc, the IUCN said. “This gives us a critical window for action for us to scale up conservation efforts and climate action to prevent the worst outcomes from occurring,” said Gudka, who is also research director at Coastal Oceans Research and Development in the Indian Ocean (CORDIO) East Africa, a conservation organisation. “The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people,” he said. IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar said it was  “not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover”. “We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them,” she said in a statement. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: France hands out swift verdicts in fast-track justice after riots
description: French courts have swiftly handed out verdicts, including orders to serve jail time, in fast-track justice for defendants accused over the rioting that erupted on the sidelines of protests at the weekend. The government says the accelerated legal processes are needed to restore order after some of the worst urban violence in recent years on Saturday. But courts are also overwhelmed, while some lawyers say the scale of the hearings reeks of state repression. French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said on Thursday that courts have sent 217 people to prison to serve jail terms over the rioting, out of some 2,700 people detained since Saturday, and added the figure will continue to rise as more hearings take place. Mathilde B., a student, 19, and 20-year-old Francois D., who said he wants to be a mountain guide, had come to Paris on Saturday from Auxerre, a city southeast of the capital. But police found a knuckleduster and switchblade in the young man’s bag and found the pair had discussed “guerrilla warfare” and “beating up riot police” on social media. Mathilde B. received a five-month suspended prison sentence but Francois D., however, was sent to jail immediately as part of an eight-month sentence, with two months to be served in custody. Tristan Lawless, a lawyer at the bar in Melun south of Paris, said he was defending a client for whom prosecutors had demanded a five-month sentence with immediate custody. He said the trial was taking place “on the basis of a 50-page case file that, in my view, was put together in haste, with reports that are often vague and lacking detail” and alleged his client had been beaten in custody. ‘Pressure on judges’ Darmanin said on Thursday that of the 217 sent to jail “half had no criminal record”, adding that “in general these are men aged between 18 to 25”. France’s Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin leaves after attending the weekly cabinet meeting at the Elysee Palace in Paris on October 22, 2026. — AFP One of the most longstanding and hyperactive members of the government, Darmanin, a former interior minister, is taking a high profile as Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s cabinet seeks to show it is in control. Once seen as having presidential ambitions himself, he is a leading supporter of former centre-right premier Edouard Philippe who is seen as one of the few candidates capable of defeating far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen in next year’s elections. “We’re here to firmly oppose what we see as an attempt by Gerald Darmanin to make the justice system more punitive,” said Paris lawyer Romain Ruiz, a member of the “Colere noire” (Black anger) collective which is highly critical of the judicial system. He accused Darmanin of “putting pressure on judges in pursuit of harsher penalties” and “publicly celebrating the imprisonment of young people”. “We will never accept that the justice system should become an arm of repression.” ‘Extremely firm’ Manuel, a 21-year-old cook from central France with no prior criminal record, said he had come to Paris “on a whim” to celebrate his birthday with a friend. But police who stopped him on Saturday close to the starting point of a demonstration found several glass bottles, some rags, and a lighter — what the prosecutor described as “the perfect kit” for a Molotov cocktail. He was sentenced to two months in prison and another six suspended. Souleymane, a 19-year-old from Ivory Coast without valid residency in France, was arrested in northern Paris while allegedly trying to steal a scooter after storming a corner shop. Convicted three times previously, he was sentenced to eight months in prison and taken into custody. Julien M., 27, a video artist from southeast France, is accused of hurling a traffic cone which just missed a policeman. He vowed that the protest would be his last and the court set him free under judicial control until a trial at the end of November. “Prosecutors and judges are imprisoning people who, until now, were not known to the judiciary and are first offenders,” said Darmanin. “It shows that the decisions of the judiciary are being applied in an extremely firm way.”

title: China bets on manufactured water, and wants to sell it to the world
description: China is emerging as a major supplier of water technology to parched countries across Asia, the Middle East and Africa, as shrinking natural supplies at home push Beijing to invest heavily in manufactured freshwater, industry experts say. Chinese firms are selling desalination membranes, filtration equipment and engineering services to Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, often through the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), which connects Chinese capital and infrastructure projects to developing markets. Even Gulf states, long desalination pioneers, are turning to Chinese manufacturers to produce equipment at scale. China exported more than $2 billion of water filtering and purifying machinery in 2025, up 25 per cent from $1.6bn in 2020, according to UN Comtrade . Vontron Technology said it shipped more than 30,000 seawater desalination membranes to BRI countries last year, enough for more than 300,000 tons of daily capacity. In January, PowerChina said it was building a water supply project in Tanzania to serve more than 450,000 people. At home, Beijing has made water security a strategic priority. Spending on water conservancy has grown faster than military spending since 2015, according to China Water Risk (CWR), a Hong Kong-based think tank. It now exceeds 1.2 trillion yuan ($170bn) a year, which CWR says rivals China’s central military budget. A crisis at home The push is rooted in domestic risk. In August, a massive collapse of ice and rock near the border between Nepal and Tibet showed how volatile natural water sources are becoming. Tibet’s “water towers” feed headwaters for nearly 2bn people across South, Southeast and East Asia, and climate change is eroding them. Meanwhile, severe over-extraction in northern China has depleted groundwater and left key farming regions with systemic deficits. “We could see peak water by 2050 across 10 major river systems that provide water to one in two Asians as glacier melt peaks and river flows decline,” CWR said. Peak water is the tipping point where flows from natural water sources reach a maximum and thereafter enter continual decline. “This will put almost half the GDP of 16 countries at risk, including China, CWR said. Benjamin Horton, dean of the School of Energy and Environment at City University of Hong Kong, said China’s ability to develop water technology at scale could cut costs for other water-stressed countries. He said Beijing could become Asia’s leading provider of practical water security solutions. “Through the Belt and Road Initiative, there is likely to be continued demand for hydropower, desalination, flood forecasting, irrigation, wastewater treatment, and climate-resilient infrastructure,” he said. Water as national security In July, China rolled out new regulations under its Five-Year Plan that treat water as a pillar of national security and economic self-reliance, not just an environmental issue. Surface water supplies about 80pc of China’s freshwater, while recycled water, desalinated seawater and harvested rainwater provide just 3pc to 4pc. Authorities have pledged to raise that share. The South-North Water Transfer Project moves billions of cubic meters from the Yangtze to the dry north, but it is constrained by energy costs and shrinking surpluses in the warming Yangtze basin. Saleh Al Khabti, China president of Saudi developer Acwa, said costs are rising and quality is deteriorating in some areas. China operated 167 seawater desalination projects at the end of 2025, with total capacity of 3,076,805 tonnes a day, up 221,283 tonnes from 2024, according to the Ministry of Natural Resources. State media put the average production cost at 4 to 8 yuan per cubic meter. Industry reports expect the market to grow from $1.84bn in 2024 to $4.66bn in 2033, or about 11pc a year. Hurdles remain, including the scale of investment and the central planning needed for multi-city conveyance grids, while public attitudes also pose a challenge. Khabti said many Chinese still view drinking desalinated water as taboo, though local governments are keen to build capacity. Foreign players buying in Khabti said more than 90pc of the renewable equipment Acwa procures comes from Chinese manufacturers, and the company buys about 70pc of its global water equipment from Chinese suppliers. Acwa has pledged to invest up to $30bn in China by 2030, working with firms including PowerChina and China Energy Engineering Corporation. It plans to spend at least $15bn a year on Chinese equipment over the next three years across renewables, green hydrogen and desalination. Khabti expects Chinese membrane makers to catch up fast. “It took us 15 years to reach where we are today with our partners,” he said. He thinks Chinese original equipment manufacturers could match that level in two to three years, and he expects desalination to follow wind and solar as “a big area of exports.” “We’re very bullish about China,” he said. “Once it’s there, China will be the leader.”

title: Govt loans turn out to be stimulant for real estate
description: KARACHI: Although banks are not ready to extend housing loans to applicants without complete documentation, builders are almost unanimous that the sector had picked up over the last 12 months. According to them, the Prime Minister’s housing scheme, which provides loans of up to Rs10 million on easy instalments, has stimulated the construction industry. “Most people can’t buy even an apartment since the purchasing price is out of reach of the middle class. The housing sch­eme has provided liquidity and purchasing has picked up,” according to Hassan Bakhshi, chairman of the Association of Builders and Developers (Abad). The country has been facing a shortage of houses while the cost of construction has gone up many times over the last five years. According to an estimate, the country requires up to 10 million houses at a time when 48 per cent of Pakistanis are living below the poverty line. Banks wary of giving loans as most projects are illegal A builder said that after release of liquidity for housing schemes, a number of people in the business have been able to recover their investments stuck in apartments that were not booked earlier as people had no money. “Banks have not issued loans as much as we were expecting, but they have some real issues,” said Mr Bakhshi. “Banks don’t issue loans unless documentation is complete.” “Most people start work on their homes without a proper design and approval of the Sindh Building Control Authority. Banks don’t consider these projects for loans,” he added. Hassan Bakhshi was, however, hopeful that the construction industry would soon pick up and it would, in turn, jumpstart over 70 allied industries. He said outflow of money from Pakistan to Dubai for purchase of property has declined as buyers divert their cash into real estate at home. The growth in construction during the six quarters from FY25 to FY26 was amazing, shooting from a negative growth to as high as 19.2pc. The State Bank recently reported that the growth rate of the construction industry was negative 3.3pc during the first quarter of FY25, but it shot up to 17.6pc in the fourth quarter of the same fiscal year. The growth rate in the first quarter of FY26 was 19.2pc, while the first half of the same fiscal year recorded growth of 14.6pc. Apna Ghar Programme The prime minister’s Ghar Ho Tu Apna scheme, launched in September last year, created demand for housing. The scheme offers subsidised financing at a fixed rate of five per cent, with markup subsidy paid by the government. According to an SBP report, construction activity had picked up pace following “some favourable developments”. The Public Sector Development Programme spending grew by 41.8pc in the first half of FY26, compared to a decline of 1.1pc in the corresponding period of last year. Prices of construction material have fallen considerably. But builders deny that prices have come down. Correction in prices Dubai, the most attractive place for buying and selling properties, lost its charm with the outbreak of the US-Iran war . Investors feel their liquidity in Dubai is stuck while the future is uncertain. Since the outflow of money for investing in Dubai properties has suddenly stopped, people flush with cash found it prudent to invest in real estate at home, which pushed up property prices in areas like Defence Society by up to 60pc. “The dust has settled now and a correction of up to 20pc in prices of properties in Defence has been noted over the last one month,” said Mr Bakhshi. Property prices have risen in almost all areas in Karachi, which serves as a barometer for the entire country, because people find no other alternative in the midst of the Gulf war. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Tech companies eye US market
description: WASHINGTON: Pakistani technology companies are seeking to expand their business with American clients by offering specialised services and products, as changing US immigration policies complicate the movement of foreign professionals. The opportunities were discussed at Pakistan-US Tech Connect 2026, a day-long business networking event hosted by the Pakistani embassy on Wednesday. Sixteen Pakistani technology companies met American business representatives and industry experts to explore partnerships and develop lasting commercial relationships. Organised with Pakistan’s Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication, the Pakistan Software Export Board (PSEB) and OPEN Global, the event featured companies working in artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data analytics, financial technology and healthcare technology. Participants stressed that Pakistani firms needed to move beyond routine IT services and competition based mainly on labour costs. Developing proprietary intellectual property, scalable products and specialised expertise would help them capture more value in international markets. Sofyan Yusufi, senior vice-president at Oracle, emphasised the importance of understanding American business culture, strengthening technical skills and building teams that reflected US market expectations. “If you survive in the Pakistani market, you can survive anywhere,” he said, according to notes from the discussion. Mr Yusufi also stressed the importance of including women in technology teams seeking American business, suggesting that an exclusively male team could indicate a limited understanding of the US market. Imran Aftab of 10Pearls highlighted the need to improve Pakistan’s education system and prepare younger generations for changes in technology, business and employment. Rebecka Zavaleta, co-founder and chief executive of PAISMO, described entrepreneurship as “a relationship with fear”. She also emphasised the need for businesses to adapt as global events unfold rather than wait for crises to end. Participants discussed the importance of tailoring products and services to customer requirements, citing demand for customised suits as an example of Pakistan’s potential to provide specialised solutions rather than compete solely on price. PSEB Chief Executive Faisal Jeddy said North America was critical to Pakistan’s IT industry. Of the $4.6 billion in IT exports recorded during the period cited at the event, 80 per cent came from North America, he said. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Middle East tensions dent investor confidence
description: KARACHI: The Pakis­tan Stock Exchange (PSX) failed to sustain its overnight recovery on Thurs­day, as escalating tensions in the Middle East shattered investor confidence, sparking fears of prolonged conflict, surging oil prices and rising inflation that thr­­­­eaten macroeconomic stability. Topline Securities Ltd said the benchmark KSE-100 index witnessed a sharp sell-off, shedding 2,006.67 points, or 1.21 per cent, to close at 163,924.32, as escalating geopolitical tensions and rising international oil prices weighed on investor sentiment. The benchmark initially touched an intraday high of 166,180.32, gaining 249 points, before plunging to a low of 163,782.42, losing 2,148 points, reflecting heightened volatility and mounting selling pressure. Persistent geopolitical uncertainty, along with concerns over rising oil prices and their potential impact on Pakistan’s economic outlook, kept investors on the defensive. The absence of positive catalysts further dampened sentiment, and selling pressure intensified as the session progressed. Index plunges 2,006 points as oil surge risks economic stability Engro Holdings, United Bank, Hub Power, Habib Bank, Pakistan Telecomm­unication Company, Lucky Cement, Fauji Fertiliser, Attock Refinery, National Bank and Pakistan Petrol­eum emerged as the major laggards, collectively dragging the benchmark down by about 1,151 points and intensifying the market’s downward momentum. Ali Najib, Deputy Head of Trading at Arif Habib Ltd, said international oil prices surged amid heightened geopolitical tensions after fresh Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia. Fears of a broader regional conflict and prolonged disruptions to Middle Eastern energy supplies weighed on investor sentiment, raising concerns over a higher energy import bill and mounting pressure on the country’s external account. On the corporate front, key banks announced their 9MCY26 results, with Habib Bank, Meezan Bank and MCB Bank reporting earnings per share of Rs36.84, Rs41.02 and Rs37.26, respectively. Investor participation re­­m­­ained moderate, with tot­al trading volume dipping 3.37pc to 367 million shares and turnover falling 15.42pc to Rs17.9bn. Pakis­t­an Refinery led the volume charts with 25.8m shares. The session ended bearish, with the benchmark ex­­t­­­­ending its losses amid persistent external headwinds. Analysts expect the market to remain sensitive to geopolitical developments and international oil price movements, with inv­e­­stors likely to stay cautious until greater clarity emerges. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: Seized goods auction goes digital
description: ISLAMABAD: The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has introduced an electronic auction system to dispose of seized and confiscated goods, allowing registered bidders to participate online for a minimum registration fee of Rs25,000. The new mechanism allows a 72-hour online bidding period, electronic payment of auction proceeds and digital release of goods to successful bidders. The rules were notified through SRO 1889 of 2026 on Thursday. Under the new rules, any person holding a valid CNIC or NICOP can register electronically as a bidder through the FBR’s auction module upon payment of a one-time registration fee of not less than Rs25,000. Upon registration, each bidder will receive a unique identification number. An authorised Inland Revenue officer may reject an application on valid grounds, which must be recorded in writing. The electronic platform will handle registration, goods listings, bidding, approvals, payments, deliveries and auction record-keeping. New rules enable online bidding, electronic payments and online record-keeping The rules apply to confiscated goods and seized goods cleared for disposal under an adjudication order. The custodian must upload the inventory, photographs and relevant documents to the electronic auction module and arrange physical inspections for prospective bidders. Before initiating an auction, the authorised officer will verify the legal status of goods, including any judicial stay order, available release or redemption options and restrictions on their disposal. Goods subject to a judicial stay cannot be auctioned until the order ceases to operate or is withdrawn. The reserve price for each lot will be fixed on the recommendation of a three-member valuation committee comprising an additional commissioner, deputy commissioner and assistant commissioner of Inland Revenue. The committee will set minimum prices based on declared sales tax invoice values, printed retail prices, customs-assessed values or market quotations, depending on the type of goods. It will also consider depreciation, physical condition and remaining shelf life. If goods remain unsold in three consecutive auctions, the committee may reduce the reserve price by up to 10pc of the reference reserve price at a time. Under the bidding mechanism, goods will remain available for online bidding for 72 hours from receipt of the first bid. The system will automatically display the highest valid bid and maintain an electronic record of each offer, including the bidder’s identification and submission time. The authorised officer will process the highest offer within 72 hours of the close of bidding. Ordinarily, bids below the reserve price will not be accepted. However, the Commissioner Inland Revenue may approve a lower offer, subject to recorded reasons, provided it is not less than 80pc of the reserve price. The notification also allows the Chief Commissioner Inland Revenue to approve lower bids. Successful bidders will be required to deposit the entire accepted bid amount, along with applicable taxes, duties and charges, within seven days of electronic communication of acceptance. Payment will be made through designated electronic channels using a payment slip identification number (PSID) or another method specified by the FBR. Goods will not be released until full payment has been verified. Published in Dawn, October 23rd, 2026

title: PTCL Group posts Rs4.7bn profit
description: ISLAMABAD: PTCL Group posted a net profit of Rs4.7 billion as its revenue exceeded Rs304bn during the July-September period of calendar year 2026. The group comprises three entities — Pakistan Telecommunication Com­­­pany Ltd, the merged telecom company (Ufone and Telenor) and U Microfinance Bank (Ubank). Announcing the financial results on Thursday, PTCL Chief Executive Officer Nadeem Khan said the company posted a 343pc surge in its net profit to Rs3bn. Mr Khan said the group’s profitability was expected to improve as the cost of doing business was at its highest level, including high electricity charges, fuel prices, and other inflationary impacts. “We are continuously pursuing the government to award an industrial electricity tariff to the telecom sector instead of the commercial tariff. This will help expand telecom infrastructure to remote areas,” he said. The mobile business, including the merged telecom company, saw revenue rise 139pc over the same period last year, while operating profit stood at Rs33.5bn. Chief Operating Officer of the merged telecom company, Atif Raza, said the new telco was integrating and rebranding. Around 40pc of Ufone and Telenor infrastructure had been integrated, benefiting about 70pc of its 76 million customers, he said. Ubank generated revenue of Rs18.3bn and reported an operating profit during the period, compared to an operating loss in the corresponding period last year. title: Mir Raza murder case: Sindh govt asks agencies, Sindh Rangers to nominate JIT members
description: The Sindh government has written to the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), the Intelligence Bureau (IB), the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency and the Sindh Rangers to nominate members to a joint investigation team (JIT), recommended by a judicial panel , to investigate Mir Raza Ali’s murder, it emerged on Saturday. The 25-year-old businessman had gone missing on July 28 after leaving his home in PECHS, and his body, bearing a gunshot wound, was found in the bushes in Gulistan-i-Jauhar a day later. In its 62-page report , submitted to the government on October 15, a commission had recommended forming a JIT, calling it a “most viable path” to mitigate ongoing reputational damage to the Sindh government. Sindh High Court judge Justice Omar Sial, who headed the single-member commission, recommended integrating senior representatives from the ISI, IB, Sindh Rangers, and the NCCIA in the JIT to “ensure an impartial, comprehensive, and credible resolution”. The commission had also recommended West Deputy Inspector General of Police (DIG) Irfan Baloch to lead the team. Acting on the commission’s directives, the Sindh Home Minister, on Thursday, announced that the JIT would be formed under the DIG Baloch, and the summary had been sent to the chief minister. The letters, dated October 23, were sent through the Sindh Home Department and seen by Dawn . They requested the ISI, IB, NCCIA and Sindh Rangers to nominate a senior officer, not below the rank of BS-18, to serve on the JIT headed by DIG Baloch to investigate Mir Raza’s murder. The letters requested the aforementioned authorities to nominate their representatives within seven days so that the JIT could commence its work. In its letter to the NCCIA, the Home Department specifically requested a senior official with “expertise in digital forensics, as the investigation involves the analysis of mobile phones, Apple Watch, iCloud, social media and cryptocurrency (Binance) records”. Letter to IGP for action against officers The provincial government, through its Home Department, also wrote to the Sindh inspector general of police (IGP), asking him to take action against police officials found guilty of negligence by the judicial commission. “This case demonstrates an epic failure by the police in their investigation,” declared the 62-page report submitted by Justice Sial. “The police breached all required procedures, both knowingly and unknowingly, necessary to withstand judicial scrutiny and a successful prosecution,” the report stated. It said the police investigation “failed in its most basic duty: to establish the truth”. According to the commission, an active cover-up in the initial stages of the investigation cannot be conclusively ruled out. It noted that senior police officers swept clear investigative lapses under the carpet, without acknowledging them, addressing them, or even attempting to do so. “Dozens of police officers – authorised and unauthorised – were involved in collecting evidence in this case, approaching and interrogating crucial persons, and in most cases not documenting it in any manner,” it said, adding that, therefore, no officer was willing to take responsibility for the lapses. Listing its observations for certain police officials involved in the case, the judicial panel identified “criminal negligence” on the part of Station House Officer (SHO) Adeel Afzal of Ferozabad police station. It also found criminal negligence by Sub-inspector Shabbir Leghari, the first investigating officer (IO) in the case, and called for disciplinary proceedings against him and his suspension. Dr Osama Sheikh suspended In its report, the judicial panel had called out “extreme immaturity” and “childish behaviour” of Medico-Legal Officer (MLO) Dr Osama Sheikh, who conducted the first medico-legal examination , whose findings were later proven incorrect after a second autopsy . “Overconfidence. Unprofessional conduct not befitting a medical professional. Must not be assigned medico-legal duties unless he has undergone at least two years of rigorous academic and practical training,” the commission observed. In a letter to the Sindh health secretary, the provincial government conveyed the decision of its sub-committee, constituted to implement the recommendations of the judicial commission, in light of the commission’s observations. Under the decision, Dr Osama would be suspended and proceeded against under the E&D (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules. He would also be sent for training, as recommended by the commission. Request to interior ministry The single-member judicial commission had stated that it did not have investigative powers and that it was difficult to conclusively determine whether an active cover-up had occurred. The commission noted that “certain inexplicable actions are difficult to justify and raise the possibility that one may have occurred”. Therefore, it recommended that a high-level committee, preferably headed by the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), be constituted to initiate criminal proceedings against any police officials found culpable. Acting on the commission’s recommendations, the Sindh government also wrote to the Ministry of Interior. In its letter, the provincial government requested the FIA to nominate a senior officer, not below the rank of BS-20 and with expertise in investigations, to head the committee. DIG Baloch and Special Branch DIG Naeem Ahmed Sheikh would serve as its members. Examination of police officers A one-member committee comprising Additional IGP Counterterrorism Department (CTD) Sindh Zulfiqar Ali Larik had also been notified to examine each of the officers named in the commission’s report. DIG Baloch would assist the committee. According to a notification, the committee had the following terms of reference (TORs): To examine each of the officers/officials named in the report of the commission of inquiry and assess their leadership qualities and efficiency in light of the specific observations recorded against them by the Commission; To evaluate their overall policing performance; To further probe the role of Inspector Ghaus with regard to the burning of the crime scene; and To submit its report, with findings and recommendations in respect of each officer/official, to the Sindh IGP.

title: Trump’s threat to strike Iran raises public concerns, congressional questions
description: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump has renewed his threat of military action against Iran, raising questions about public support for the war and Congress’s ability to restrain further escalation . With midterm elections approaching on November 3, polls show widespread dissatisfaction with the war , particularly over rising fuel prices and the risk to American troops. Reports of renewed US-Israeli military planning have also raised concerns about possible strikes after the elections. Trump made his latest threat at a rally in Florida on Friday. “We may do another little Epic Fury ,” he said, referring to the US military operation against Iran. He gave no details about when another operation might begin. The remarks followed an ABC News report on Thursday that the US military and the Israel Defence Forces had drawn up options for renewed joint strikes. The report cited two Israeli sources familiar with the plans, who said the strikes would most likely take place after the midterms. White House spokesperson Anna Kelly, however, told ABC News that “the United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections.” The reports indicate that further military action is being considered, but they do not establish that Trump has ordered an attack. Negotiations remain another possibility. Strategic choices and political pressure In an analysis published on October 23, James M. Lindsay, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, outlined three options for Trump: escalate the conflict, negotiate with Tehran or maintain the current position. “All three options have substantial downsides and a questionable likelihood of succeeding,” Lindsay wrote. Further attacks could increase pressure on Iran but might prolong the conflict without securing a political settlement. Negotiations would require the two sides to bridge their differences, while maintaining the current position could leave the conflict unresolved. Andrew Payne, research director for Europe, Russia and the Americas at Chatham House, argued in an October 15 analysis that foreign policy could play an unusual role in this year’s midterm elections. The war’s economic consequences could influence voters who might otherwise focus primarily on domestic issues, particularly the cost of living. Public opinion turns against the war A Pew Research Centre survey conducted from September 28 to October 4 among 5,062 US adults found that 65 per cent disapproved of Trump’s handling of the military action against Iran, while 33pc approved. The survey also found that 73pc were extremely or very concerned about higher fuel prices, and 71pc about American troops being wounded or killed. Nearly half, 47pc, expected the military action to continue for more than another year. A separate Associated Press -NORC poll published on October 22 found that roughly seven in 10 registered voters wanted the next Congress to make ending the Iran war a top priority. About eight in 10 gave similar priority to reducing the cost of living. The poll surveyed 1,119 US adults from October 8 to 12. The findings point to pressure on the administration to address the war’s duration and economic consequences. However, dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the conflict does not necessarily mean that voters would oppose every possible military operation. Can Congress restrain Trump? Congress can scrutinise military operations, hold oversight hearings and use its control over federal spending to influence the course of the war. Lawmakers can also invoke the War Powers Resolution to challenge military action. The resolution requires the president to notify Congress in certain circumstances when US forces enter hostilities. It also establishes procedures for lawmakers to consider whether military action should continue. Funding could become particularly important if the conflict expands. Congress can approve, restrict or condition spending for military operations, potentially increasing the political cost of a prolonged campaign. The extent of congressional pressure would depend partly on whether Republicans remain united behind Trump. If some Republican lawmakers join Democrats in challenging the war, the administration could face greater scrutiny of its objectives and plans for ending the conflict. Even a congressional challenge, however, would not automatically prevent the president from ordering another strike. The question after November 3 The immediate question is whether Trump will maintain his stated position against attacking Iran before the midterms. The larger issue is whether the election results will alter the political constraints on his decisions. The reported military planning and Trump’s latest remarks keep the prospect of renewed strikes alive, but neither establishes that an attack has been scheduled. A change in control of either chamber of Congress could affect oversight and funding debates, although it would not automatically prevent further military action. Whether the combined pressures of public dissatisfaction, economic concerns and congressional scrutiny lead Trump towards negotiations or renewed strikes remains unclear.

title: Pakistan denounces ‘heinous’ church attack in Jordan, reiterates condemnation of terrorism
description: Pakistan has strongly condemned the “heinous terrorist attack” on a funeral procession at a church in Jordan’s Karak Governorate, reiterating its condemnation of terrorism in all its forms and manifestations. Gunmen killed at least seven people and wounded dozens at a church in southern Jordan on Friday. According to reports, the assailants stormed the compound of a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak Governorate and opened fire. According to a statement issued by the Foreign Office (FO), Pakistan extended its heartfelt condolences to the government and people of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, particularly the bereaved families, and expressed its wishes for the speedy recovery of those injured. “Pakistan stands in firm solidarity with the brotherly people of Jordan in their fight against terrorism, and reiterates its strongest condemnation of terrorism in all its forms and manifestations”, the statement added. The incident occurred when gunmen got out of a vehicle and opened fire during a funeral procession, Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said in a statement, adding that a manhunt was under way for the perpetrators. “The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation,” King Abdullah II said in a post on X. “We will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation.” According to images from state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka , the king arrived in Karak on Friday evening. After authorities gave a death toll of six, Director of Public Security Major General Abdullah Al-Maaytah said it had risen to seven with 34 injured, 27 of whom were still receiving treatment. Footage aired by Al-Mamlaka showed two gunmen dressed in casual clothes and brandishing pistols, with a third carrying a long gun as they opened fire on the church. A witness said the gunmen fired continuously for five minutes before fleeing. Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said.

title: 4 children killed as van plunges into ravine in Neelum Valley
description: MUZAFFARABAD: Four children were killed and three other people were injured when a van carrying them to a madrasah plunged into a ravine in the upper reaches of Neelum Valley on Saturday, officials said. Neelum Valley District Disaster Management Officer Akhtar Ayoub said the van was travelling from Nagdar, about 22 kilometres from the district headquarters of Athmuqam, via the Keran bypass link road when it plunged into a ravine. “The accident occurred around 8:30am near Ghorray Nakkah Morr in Nagdar, barely half a kilometre into the journey, as the driver negotiated a sharp bend,” he said. The van plunged more than 500 metres off the road into a rocky ravine, killing three children on the spot and initially injuring four other occupants. One of the injured children later died at the District Headquarters Hospital in Athmuqam, Ayoub said. The injured were later shifted to Muzaffarabad for treatment due to their critical condition, he added. Expressing grief over the loss of young lives, Legislative Assembly Speaker Chaudhry Tariq Farooq extended his condolences to the bereaved families and prayed for the speedy recovery of the injured. “Deeply saddened by the loss of precious young lives in the tragic accident in Neelum Valley today. My heartfelt condolences go out to the bereaved families, and I pray for the speedy recovery of the injured,” he wrote on X. “Mountain roads demand utmost caution; even a momentary lapse can have tragic consequences. Please drive carefully,” he added. A similar accident occurred in April when three people were killed, and 10 others were injured when a passenger van plunged into a deep ravine in the Maidan Nambatai area. On May 11, four people, including two women, were killed and two others injured after a passenger jeep plunged hundreds of feet into a rocky streambed.

title: Israel launches major West Bank operation after soldiers killed
description: Israel’s military launched an operation in the occupied West Bank on Friday, which it said would last several days and include searches and building demolitions, after gunmen killed two soldiers days ahead of Israeli elections in which security has been a key focus. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is locked in a tight race to keep his job in Tuesday’s vote, having campaigned on promises to keep Israelis safe , and he and his right-wing allies visited the scene of the attack to pledge an even harder line on West Bank militancy. Security forces were searching targets and questioning Palestinians to “locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure” in the Hebron area from where they said the attackers had emerged, according to a joint statement from the Israeli military and Shin Bet domestic security agency. Israeli forces were also “demolishing illegal structures that could pose a security threat at the site of the encounter”, they said, adding that “counterterrorism operations” were underway at dozens of locations. The operation “is expected to continue for several days,” the statement, released late on Friday, said. Hamas, without claiming responsibility, praised Friday’s fatal attack on two Israeli soldiers as a “heroic operation” and called on supporters to carry out more. A Hebron-based AFP photographer heading to another assignment witnessed the gun battle break out at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint between the soldiers and two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle. Israeli forces eventually shot dead the attackers. Netanyahu credited the soldiers with having “prevented what could have been a major attack”, and ordered a lockdown in the West Bank. Visiting Hebron, the premier said he and Defence Minister Israel Katz were “considering a very extensive IDF operation in Judea and Samaria, such as has not been carried out since” the 1967 war. The first step would see Israeli forces “enter the neighbourhood from which the terrorists came, evacuate the residents, go from house to house, and destroy the terrorist infrastructure,” he claimed. The military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank, he said, the scene of a large-scale operation launched in January 2025 that the United Nations said forcibly displaced thousands. Israeli rights group B’Tselem called for urgent international pressure to prevent Israel from pursuing “plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, through a spokesman, voiced concern over Israeli closures that affect Palestinian livelihoods and called for a halt to violence on all sides. ‘Exactly like Gaza’ Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a large-scale military offensive in the West Bank “ exactly like in Gaza ”. National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir said the Ramallah-based “Palestinian Authority must be dismantled”. No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority — which exercises limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank — was connected to Friday’s attack. Both Ben Gvir and Smotrich are especially vocal supporters of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which have proliferated under Netanyahu’s government but are illegal under international law. Israel vowed to obliterate the group in the wake of the October 7, 2023 attack . Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is Netanyahu’s top rival in the upcoming vote, said he was praying for soldiers wounded in Friday’s shooting. The operation comes as tensions soar in the West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters. According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces and settlers have killed 1,117 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023. Israeli figures show that at least 51 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.

title: Haris Rauf calls for middle-over breakthroughs as ODI scores soar
description: One-day International cricket has gone through changes over the years, but one of the aspects of the game that has continued to be crucial is the importance of taking wickets in the middle overs. In the span of the last three years, which included Pakistan’s dismal 2023 World Cup campaign in India, the national side’s bowlers have struggled to strike as often as they would have liked in the middle overs. Haris Rauf, who has featured for Pakistan in most of the matches through this period, is well aware of the team’s shortcomings as they look forward to the next edition of the World Cup, set to be co-hosted by South Africa, Namibia and Zimbabwe in 2027. Pakistan’s bowlers have averaged 4.11 dismissals between overs 11 and 40 in ODIs since the start of 2023. The figures underline the challenge facing a side that has often depended on early breakthroughs and late-innings bowling to contain opponents. Speaking to reporters at Gaddafi Stadium on Friday, ahead of Sunday’s tri-series match against England, Haris acknowledged the importance of striking in the middle overs, warning that allowing batters to settle could leave the bowling side struggling to recover. “If you do not take wickets in the middle overs, you will struggle as a team,” the fast bowler said. “If their middle-order batters or openers remain at the crease until the end, they can hurt you.” Pakistan have made a promising start to the ongoing tri-series, beating Sri Lanka by 37 runs and England by 87 in their first two matches. But the contest between England and Sri Lanka in Rawalpindi on Thursday, when the latter chased down a target of 430 after England posted 429-4, offered a reminder of how little room for error bowlers have on batting-friendly surfaces. Haris believes the modern game demands more from both departments, with teams needing to prepare for totals well beyond 300. “Nowadays, we may have to score 350-plus runs ourselves at the World Cup and chase totals of 350-plus as well,” he said. “The support for bowlers is a little less, but you have to keep working on your own skills and make the most of situations when conditions favour you.” One potential source of assistance is reverse swing, particularly with the revised ODI playing conditions introduced in July last year. Under the change, two new balls are used until the end of the 34th over, after which the fielding side chooses one ball to be used at both ends for overs 35 to 50. Previously, a separate ball was used from each end throughout the innings, limiting the extent to which either could age. Haris said the older ball could offer an advantage during daytime matches, when conditions were more conducive to reverse swing, but added that dew could reduce its effectiveness in night games. The opportunity, however, is not enough on its own. Pakistan must translate any assistance into wickets, particularly during the middle overs, when established batters can accelerate and put the bowling attack under pressure. Haris’ own recent domestic performances suggest that he has been working towards greater consistency and endurance. The 32-year-old represented Pakistan Television in four matches of the ongoing President’s Trophy Grade-I competition, taking 18 wickets, averaging 20.11, including two four-wicket hauls and a best return of 5-34. For a bowler whose rise was built largely on raw pace, domestic cricket has provided an opportunity to sharpen his control and build the capacity to bowl longer spells. Haris, who emerged from Pakistan’s tape-ball circuit before earning recognition through Lahore Qalandars’ development programme, made his international debut in 2020. “Domestic cricket is just as important as international cricket,” he said. “You go there and work on your mistakes. I tried to bowl longer spells, and having played four-day cricket, I feel that one-day cricket is not as difficult for me now. Your control over line and length improves.” The stint has also prompted Haris to reiterate his willingness to return to Test cricket, a format that became the centre of a dispute between him and the then chief selector Wahab Riaz in late 2023. Haris withdrew from Pakistan’s tour of Australia after initially being considered for selection, citing concerns over workload and fitness. Wahab said the team had planned to use him as an impact bowler in short spells and maintained that the management had received assurances about his availability. The disagreement escalated in February 2024, when the PCB terminated Haris’ central contract, citing his refusal to tour. Haris said he had not been ready for the demands of Test cricket at the time but was now working towards making himself available if Pakistan needed him. “I am looking at myself for that role as well. If the team needs a fast bowler or someone who can provide pace, why should I not make myself available?” he said. “If I get the opportunity to play red-ball cricket for Pakistan, I will certainly take it.” For now, his immediate task remains helping Pakistan sustain their early momentum in the tri-series – in two matches of which he has bagged four wickets at 20 – while addressing a weakness that has persisted across formats and campaigns. Haris insisted that criticism over runs conceded would not deter him, arguing that the demands of modern cricket meant even the best bowlers could have difficult days. “Pace is very important. I work on my fitness and try to maintain it during the off-season,” he said. “I have managed to maintain my pace, and I will continue trying to do so.” With the 2027 World Cup approaching, Pakistan’s challenge will be to ensure that pace, reverse swing and improved preparation translate into the breakthroughs that matter most. For Haris, that begins with taking wickets when the opposition is building an innings, rather than waiting for the death overs to turn the contest.

title: France to deploy 70,000 police for fresh weekend protests
description: France will deploy about 70,000 police nationwide as it braces for new protests on Saturday after some of the worst urban violence in years erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations a week ago. Protests by high school students over learning conditions sparked a movement that has since spread nationwide, fuelled by broader anger over the rising cost of living. About 70,000 security personnel will be deployed on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at a news conference in Paris, warning that calls for violence and looting were circulating on social media. The protests have come at a critical moment for France six months ahead of elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron, with a new poll underlining far-right candidate Marine Le Pen as the frontrunner and indicating her position has been strengthened by the latest events. Adding to tensions, Le Pen is due at the weekend to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orleans, with thousands of supporters expected and local authorities fearing clashes as counter-protesters also head to the city south of Paris. Macron met representatives of secondary school pupils on Friday, but they emerged from the talks urging students to keep protesting until the government put forward concrete proposals to address their demands. Offenders jailed Macron’s government has sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations last Saturday. Courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said. On Thursday, Macron called for “the utmost severity” against “acts of delinquency”, accusing “ultra-left” groups of having sought to “bring down the republic” last weekend. An extreme-left group in western France posted on its website a call for its supporters to be “uncatchable, unpredictable, to evade the deployment” of police. Protest restrictions Authorities have stepped up security measures and imposed restrictions on protests. In Orleans, between 20,000 and 30,000 people are expected to come out against Le Pen’s National Rally party, but the gathering will be barred from the city centre, the prefecture said. In the southeastern city of Lyon, central areas will also be off-limits to demonstrators this weekend. In Paris, police overturned a previous permit for union-led protesters to march between Bastille and Nation squares in the east. The force said the parade could instead go in the afternoon along an alternative route on the southeastern edge of the city. Unions vowed to push ahead on the banned route, citing safety concerns over the alternative. Authorities in Marseille had also banned protests but announced Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an “exceptional basis” – the only one authorised in the southern Bouches-du-Rhone department. In the capital, leading museums including the Louvre will be closed on Saturday while the Art Basel art fair is being cut short. Police ‘responsibility’ The restrictions, including outright bans on protests in some cities, have drawn criticism. Amnesty International denounced what it called “a slide toward authoritarian practice”, saying the measures were “jeopardising the right to demonstrate peacefully”. About 20 percent more members of the security forces will be deployed this weekend following questions over police preparedness and intelligence gathering ahead of last week’s violence. “Police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder,” said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. She voiced alarm over reports of children being severely injured by crowd-control weapons during recent gatherings. The violence has tarnished the image of France ahead of elections that could be a turning point in its modern history, with the government’s debt pile also troubling investors. A new poll by Harris Interactive for M6/RTL made after the violence showed Le Pen soaring ahead on 33-35 percent in the first round of voting for the presidential elections. It predicted that hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon was on course to face her in the run-off where Le Pen would emerge as an easy winner on about 70 percent of the vote.

title: Fire breaks out at Hitler's mountain retreat, suspect detained: police
description: German police said Saturday they had detained a suspect following a fire at Adolf Hitler’s mountain retreat, known as the Eagle’s Nest, in the state of Bavaria. Around 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote Kehlsteinhaus residence, on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany. Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said. “A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody,” they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the blaze. Police spokeswoman Lisa Maier said firefighters struggled to tackle the blaze due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres. The building was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said. Authorities were alerted to the fire on Friday evening, when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at around 9:50pm (1950 GMT), police said. “The criminal police investigation is ongoing,” Maier added. German tabloid Bild reported that the authorities arrested a motorcyclist they came across on their way to the scene and that they suspected the fire was the result of arson. Built in the 1930s, the Eagle’s Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Germany’s bitter 20th-century history.

title: Man held for torturing female scooty rider in Lahore
description: LAHORE: The police on Friday claimed to have arrested a man who had allegedly tortured and injured a young woman riding a scooty on busy Mozang Link Road in the city. Identified as Ghulam Mustafa, the attacker was tracked down and arrested by the police with the help of data of dozens of the Punjab Safe Cities Authority (PSCA) cameras, besides using traditional investigation techniques. He was sent behind the bars after being nominated in a criminal case. A CCTV footage of the incident, which took place late on Thursday,  sparked widespread public outrage once footage was aired. The footage showed the suspect overtook the scooty rider on the busy road, placed his bike in front of her two wheeler and subjected her to brutal torture in the presence of several passersby. It was shocking to observe that none of the onlookers tried to intervene and rescue the woman. The man pulled her hair and slapped her repeatedly. As per initial police reports, the woman suffered facial injuries, including nasal bone fracture, during the brutal attack. A police official says the attacker also threw the victim’s bag on the ground that contained a laptop valuing around Rs90,000, resulting in severe damage to the laptop. The suspect later fled the scene in the presence of several onlookers, he adds. A special police team, under the supervision of Civil Lines Superintendent of Police (SP) Maniza Karamat, tracked down and arrested the suspect using modern digital tracking technology. The official says that a case has been lodged against the attacker on the complaint of the victim’s father. Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: Fuel dealers urge consumers to avoid ‘panic buying’
description: • PPDA chairman says pricing remains an issue • JI demands meeting with PM ‘this week’ to resolve levy issue ISLAMABAD: Even as talks between the Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) and the government to reduce the fuel levy remained ‘inconclusive’, petroleum dealers on Friday urged consumers not to resort to panic buying, as excessive purchases could create market distortions. Talking to reporters, Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) Chairman Malik Khuda Baksh said the delicate balance between supply and demand had been maintained efficiently by all stakeholders, including the government, industry and consumers. At the same time, he said the recent closure of the Iran border had put the liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) market under stress. “As far as petrol supply is concerned, there is a huge responsibility on consumers too, especially petrol consumers. We have seen in the past that when cars and motorcycles line up at petrol pumps, it creates artificial shortages in some areas,” the PPDA chairman said. He said reports were circulating that the country could run dry in the coming days and recalled the situation during the US invasion of Afghanistan in October 2001. “There were such reports and a brief panic in those days too, but petrol and diesel remained available in the country. Similarly, the situation remains under control now as well,” he added. Mr Baksh said refineries were operational, while both crude oil and petroleum products were being imported from Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia and Oman. “Price remains an issue, but that is a different matter,” he said. According to oil industry estimates, diesel demand during November 2026 is likely to be around 750,000 tonnes, driven by seasonal agricultural requirements. Industry sources said local refineries supplied approximately 70 per cent of the country’s diesel requirements, although the bulk of the crude oil processed by them was imported. Petrol demand for November is estimated at around 630,000 tonnes, while local production accounts for roughly 30pc of national consumption. Petroleum industry sources added that high prices and the off-peak travel season were likely to keep consumption subdued next month. Jamaat-govt talks Meanwhile, the JI called on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to announce additional relief for the public in his proposed meeting with Hafiz Naeem, and asked that the meeting be held ‘this week’. Speaking to reporters after holding talks with a government delegation led by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, JI Deputy Emir Liaqat Baloch told reporters that while the party would continue to pursue negotiations, it would not abandon the path of protest. As talks continue a technical committee comprising State Minister for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani, JI Islamabad Emir Nasrullah Randhawa and Deputy Secretary Syed Farasat Shah has been constituted and the committee would meet within two to three days to examine the outstanding issues. Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: Govt raises high-speed diesel rate by Rs1.91 per litre; petrol price unchanged at Rs377.71
WB urges Pakistan to shift from stability to growth
description: WORLD Bank official Sandeep Mahajan meets Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb.—X/ @Financegovpk • Calls for stronger investment, private sector activity • Aurangzeb stresses need to strengthen investor confidence ISLAMABAD: In what appears to be a push towards accelerating growth, the World Bank has advised Pakistan to move from stabilisation to sustainable growth, with a focus on strengthening investment and private sector activity. This marks the second such endorsement from the international financial institution, which recently commended Pakistan’s stabilisation programme and urged a shift towards sustainable growth to generate employment opportunities for the youth. The IMF has also offered similar advice to Islamabad at a recent workshop on tax reforms. World Bank Regional Practice Director for the Prosperity Vertical for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (MENAAP) Sandeep Mahajan met Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Friday. He was accompanied by Country Director Bolor­maa Amgaabazar and International Finance Corporation (IFC) Division Director Simon Andrews. An official statement said the meeting discussed Pakistan’s economic reform agenda, the transition from stabilisation to sustainable growth and priorities for strengthening inve­stment and private sector activity. Mr Mahajan congratulated Pakis­tan on restoring macroeconomic stability and commended the government’s management of the recent crisis arising from regional conflict. He noted that buffers built through stabilisation efforts and a timely policy response had helped Pakistan manage external pressures. World Bank representatives emphasised the importance of sustaining these gains through continued reforms and effective implementation. Mr Aurangzeb said the government’s priority was to make macroeconomic stability durable and translate it into sustainable, investment-led and export-driven growth. He said that Pakistan had regained access to international capital markets, including through its recent $3 billion Eurobond issuance with five-year and 10-year maturities. The minister also stressed the need to secure further credit rating upgrades, strengthen investor confidence and improve Pakistan’s sovereign credit profile.
