Mr Aurangzeb underscored the importance of a credible transition framework that maintained fiscal discipline, addressed external sector vulnerabilities and strengthened the foundations for private sector-led, responsible and sustainable growth. The discussion also covered international experience in strengthening fiscal frameworks and policy credibility to manage external risks and support investor confidence. Policy continuity was highlighted as another key requirement for sustained economic progress. The finance minister noted that investment and productivity depended on a predictable policy environment and consistent implementation. Mr Aurangzeb and the World Bank representatives also exchanged views on the government’s growth and jobs agenda, including opportunities to strengthen private sector investment, improve the regulatory environment and mobilise financing for infrastructure. The discussion covered privatisation, the importance of clear regulatory frameworks and credible post-privatisation arran­gements, as well as the potential to develop infrastructure projects through appropriate financing structures and collaboration with development partners. Both sides reaffirmed the importance of continued cooperation between Pakistan and the World Bank, with a focus on sustaining macroeconomic stability, advancing structural reforms, strengthening policy continuity and translating reform gains into investment, employment and improved economic opportunities. Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: KP governor rules out talks with ‘anti-state elements’
description: • Kundi calls for decisive action against terrorists, stronger police capacity • Says Centre ready to provide weapons, financial resources to KP police • Insists peace essential for development, investment in province CHARSADDA / PESHAWAR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi on Friday ruled out negotiations or concessions for elements who do not accept the Constitution, stressing that decisive action against terrorism and strengthening the province’s police was the only way to restoring peace. Speaking to journalists after visiting the families of CTD DSP Imranuddin Khan and Constable Kazim Jan in Charsadda, Mr Kundi said elements working against the state should not be offered concessions. He said the Pakistan Army, police and other security agencies had rendered immense sacrifices for the country’s security and stressed that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa must be freed from terrorism. Referring to a recent meeting of the National Apex Committee , the governor said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had made it clear that a policy of zero tolerance would be adopted against terrorism. He said decisive action against terrorists was necessary to restore lasting peace, adding that the public should distance itself from terrorists and refrain from providing them shelter. Mr Kundi said police and other law enforcement agencies required modern weapons and equipment to confront terrorists and that he was prepared to divert funds from his development allocation for the purpose. He added that Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had assured him that the federal government was ready to provide the police with the required weapons and financial resources. Mr Kundi said the compensation package for police personnel martyred in the line of duty had been enhanced and that police salaries were also being increased. Asked about the non-functional chief minister Sohail Afridi, Mr Kundi said Mr Afridi was in safe hands, adding that nobody could predict what would happen in the future. The governor’s adviser on information, Samar Haroon Bilour, said the police and Counter-Terrorism Department needed modern weapons, secure vehicles, tracking systems and protective equipment to improve their operational capacity. She said sustained federal support was necessary to strengthen both institutions. Earlier in the day, DSP Imranuddin and Constable Jan, who were martyred during an operation against terrorists in Karak district on Thursday, were laid to rest in their native villages in Charsadda with police honours. Mr Kundi claimed that weapons left behind following the withdrawal of international forces from Afghanistan had fallen into the hands of terrorists. He said Pakistan’s long border with Afghanistan made surveillance difficult in some areas and that terrorists possessed sophisticated weapons. Federal package Separately, addressing a news conference at Governor House in Peshawar, Mr Kundi said demands presented by the provincial advisory council at the Apex Committee meeting on Thursday had been accepted by PM Shehbaz. “Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a package of Rs160 billion for the province. To resolve issues related to gas and wheat, the prime minister directed the secretary of food department to convene a meeting soon,” he said. According to the governor, the meeting, attended by the prime minister and senior military leadership, focused on security, development and public concerns in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Mr Kundi said peace was essential for development and investment in the province. “If there is peace in the province, there will be development and investment will also come from abroad,” he said. He added that the provincial advisory council would pursue KP’s rights on the basis of facts and said talks had also been held with representatives of the Awami National Party, Jamaat-i-Islami and Qaumi Watan Party chief Aftab Ahmad Khan Sherpao. Mr Kundi said political parties needed to unite over the province’s rights. He also raised the issue of KP’s water share, insisting that the province was not receiving its due allocation under the 1991 water accord. He said the federal government had heard the province’s position and tenders for packages one and four of the Chashma Lift Canal would be issued next month. Ms Bilour said development priorities discussed with the federal government included road connectivity, educational institutions, information technology hubs and vocational training facilities. She said improving security and providing young people with better educational and employment opportunities were both necessary for the province’s long-term development. Mr Kundi said restoring peace, strengthening the police and securing the province’s constitutional and development rights were essential for KP’s future. Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: NA body summons Punjab police chief over Hina Javed murder case
description: RAWALPINDI: The National Assembly Standing Committee on Interior and Narcotics Control has summoned the Punjab inspector general of police (IGP), regional police officer (RPO), city police officer (CPO) Rawalpindi, SSP Investigation and additional inspector general of the Crime Control Department (CCD) to brief it on the investigation into the alleged brutal murder of Hina Javed. The committee meeting is scheduled for Thursday, October 29, 2026, at 2pm in the committee room at Parliament House, Islamabad. The police officials will brief committee members on the latest developments in the high-profile murder case. The Punjab government has also formed a three-member high-powered committee to review the investigation into Hina Javed’s murder. Her husband and domestic servant have been placed on judicial remand at Adiala Jail in connection with the case. The committee has already visited Rawalpindi, questioned the deceased woman’s husband and domestic servant at Adiala Jail, met her family and inspected the crime scene. The panel comprises Additional IG CCD Sohail Chatta, DIG Lahore Shoaib Khurram Janbaz and SSP Investigation Rawalpindi Saifullah. According to the postmortem and DNA report analysis , evidence collected during the investigation indicated that Hina Javed had been brutally tortured. The report noted blue marks on her hands and arms and a 27-centimetre-deep wound on her neck. The report also stated that DNA collected from bloodstains, bedsheets allegedly used in the strangulation, a door lock and a door handle matched the DNA of the domestic servant. Evidence collected for DNA testing included swabs from the deceased’s left-hand fingernails, samples taken from her body and pieces of cloth from a bedsheet bearing suspected bloodstains and spermatozoa. According to the report, the samples matched the domestic worker’s blood. A reddish piece of carpet bearing suspected stains was also recovered from the southeastern bedroom of the apartment where the crime occurred. The report said the stains matched the blood and sperm attributed to Zeeshan Arshad. The investigation has focused on the domestic servant’s alleged involvement, with the reported DNA findings forming part of the evidence under examination. Meanwhile, Hina Javed’s family has again expressed mistrust in the Rawalpindi police investigation and the claims made by the CCD chief, demanding the formation of a judicial commission to probe the murder. The family has alleged that police are protecting the main accused while holding the domestic servant responsible for the crime. The initial postmortem examination and police report stated that Hina Javed’s body was found in the washroom of her apartment with signs of torture, including a strangulation mark around her neck, an injury below her right lip and bleeding from her nose. Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: Jordan church shooting claims 7 lives
description: AMMAN: Gunmen killed at least seven people and wounded dozens at a church in southern Jordan on Friday, authorities said, with the king vowing retaliation for the rare attack on Christians in the majority Muslim kingdom. Assailants stormed the compound of a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate and opened fire, authorities said. The gunmen got out of a vehicle and started shooting during a funeral procession, the public security directorate said in a statement, adding that a manhunt was underway for the perpetrators. “The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation,” King Abdullah II said in a post on X. “We will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation.” According to images from state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka, the king arrived in Karak on Friday evening. After authorities gave a death toll of six, Director of Public Security Major General Abdullah Al-Maaytah said it had risen to seven with 34 injured, 27 of whom were still receiving treatment. Footage aired by Al-Mamlaka showed two gunmen dressed in casual clothes and brandishing pistols, with a third carrying a long gun as they opened fire on the church. A witness said the gunmen fired continuously for five minutes before fleeing. Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said. Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: Over 500 ‘illegal’ Afghans held in three provinces
description: ISLAMABAD: Undocumented Afghan nationals continue to be arrested by authorities, and a joint report of IOM and UNHCR says over the past one week, 517 Afghans were arrested from three districts of Balochistan, Sindh and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. Out of all arrests and detentions during October 11 to 17, ACC holders and undocumented Afghans from Chagai, Peshawar and Karachi represented 97 per cent of the total arrests and detentions, while Proof of Regis­tration (POR) holders represented 3 per cent. About 56pc of the total reported arrests and detentions took place in Balochistan, 34pc in Pun­jab and 10pc in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. The report says prior to 2023, there was no data collected on the arrest and detention of Afghan Citizen Card (ACC) holders or undocumented Afghan nationals. Since January 2023, IOM has started to collect the data. Findings of the report show cumulatively, from Sept 15, 2023 to Oct 17, 2026, about 2,744,068 Afghans have been sent back to their country from Pakistan. Between Oct 11 and 17, UNHCR and IOM estimate 3,883 Afghans returned through the Torkham, Chaman and Bahramcha border crossing points to Afghanistan. Between October 11 and 17, the nu­­mber of returns decreased by 10pc and deportations by 48pc — compared to the previous week of October 4 to 10, 2026 (4,295 returns including 961 deportations). Betw­een Oct 11 and 17, a total of 3,883 returns were reported, including 499 deportations. Compared to the previous week, dep­o­­rtations de­­c­­reased significantly, while returns de­­creased only moderately, report says. Among those who returned bet­we­en Oct 11 and 17, most were un­­documented (83pc) followed by ACC holders (9pc) and PoR holders (8pc). Majority of the PoR returns were processed by UNHCR through the Volu­n­tary Repatriation Centres (VRCs). Among those deported between Oct 11 and 17, most were undocumented (99pc) followed by PoR holders (1pc) and ACC holders (1pc). Since April 1, 2025, 1,890,035 Afghans returned, of which 237,387 (13pc) were deported. During the period, fear of arrest remained the main reason for return among undocumented individuals and ACC holders (95pc) as well as for PoR holders (68pc). Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: ECP proposes AI rules for parties, media, election observers
description: ISLAMABAD: The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) has proposed amendments to the codes of conduct for political parties and contesting candidates, media and election observers to protect the electoral process from the harmful effects of artificial intelligence (AI). The commission has shared the draft amendments with stakeholders and sought their feedback by Nov 20. According to a draft notification issued on Friday, the ECP cited its constitutional duty under Article 218(3) to ensure honest, just and fair elections. “Therefore, it is the core responsibility of the commission to take all necessary steps to guard against corrupt practices, which also include manipulation of the electoral process through misleading content generated using AI,” the notification said. Draft bars digitally manipulated ‘defamatory content’; feedback sought by Nov 20 Under the proposed rules, political parties and contesting candidates would be required to clearly disclose all AI-generated campaign material, including deepfake images, audio, video and synthetic voices. Robocalls and voter outreach messages using cloned voices would have to disclose their AI-generated nature at the outset. The draft prohibits AI-generated content intended to deceive voters or misrepresent individuals. It also bans false, derogatory or defamatory deepfake statements targeting candidates, party leaders, supporters, election officials, the judiciary, state functionaries or the armed forces. Political parties would be barred from using automated bots or acco­unts to artificially inflate likes, comments, shares or followers to create a false impression of public support. They would also be required to retain logs of all AI-assisted campaign content and submit them to the ECP upon request. Print, electronic and digital media outlets, as well as social media influencers, would be required to explicitly label AI-altered election content. Media houses would remain legally responsible for the factual accuracy of content produced using AI tools for translation, anchoring or analysis. The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority, the Social Media Protection and Regulatory Authority and the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency will actively monitor online platforms. They will submit compliance reports to the ECP, which retains the authority to order immediate content takedowns or re-labelling. Election observers would be required to identify and promptly report AI-generated deepfakes and disinformation campaigns directly to the ECP without further spreading the misleading material. They would also be prohibited from using AI to fabricate or embellish election photographs, videos, reports or field observations. Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia have completed ratification of Makkah defence pact: FO
description: Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have completed the ratification processes for the Makkah defence pact while Turkiye was in the process of doing so, Foreign Office (FO) spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said on Friday. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The pact has gained significance amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, and Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said earlier this week that Pakistan was providing “whatever support is needed” to defend the kingdom. Prior to that, the FO had emphasised that signing the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and committing military capabilities under it were executive functions under Pakistan’s national laws and Rules of Business and did not necessarily require parliamentary approval. Answering questions after the weekly press briefing, the FO spokesperson said that “matters related to the agreement, its ratification and operationalisation remain under discussion by the three parties”. This included discussions during the Strategic Political and Defence Committee, which recently met on Oct 5, he added. “The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement reflects the shared commitment of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye to strengthening collective defence and cooperation for regional security and stability,” Khan said. He further noted that each country followed its own constitutional and legal procedures to approve and ratify international agreements. “Pakistan and [the] Kingdom of Saudi Arabia have already completed their ratification processes, while Turkiye is undertaking the requisite procedures in accordance with its domestic legal framework,” he said. Turkiye submitted the Makkah defence pact to its parliament for ratification earlier this week. The spokesperson highlighted Pakistan’s continued commitment to the letter and spirit of the agreement, which he said “is defensive in nature, consistent with the UN Charter, and aimed at promoting regional peace, security and stability”. Answering a follow-up question regarding Article 2 of the pact, which states that an attack on one party would be considered an attack against all parties, Khan stressed again that the agreement was “essentially defensive in nature” and consistent with Article 51 of the UN Charter, which provides the right to self-defence”. “The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement reflects the shared commitment of all three parties, primarily to strengthening collective defence, deterrence, and regional stability,” he said. He added, “It is not directed against any particular country. It provides a framework for collective assistance in the event of external armed aggression against any party.” According to Khan, the “nature and extent” of any such assistance would be determined collectively by the three countries as the situation arose, “following an objective assessment of the circumstances”. To another question, he clarified that there were “no hidden provisions” in the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. “We endorse the text released in the media from the Turkish Parliament. There are no hidden provisions; the agreement is explicit and clear in its provisions and articles,” he said. Regarding the potential invocation of the agreement in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the spokesperson reiterated that “This matter has to be decided by the three partner countries in accordance with the agreement.” He also expressed Pakistan’s concern over the recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and its implications for regional peace and security. “Our position has been clear and consistent,” Khan said. “We support Yemen’s sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity, and believe that a lasting solution to the conflict can only be achieved through dialogue and a negotiated political settlement … At the same time, we unequivocally condemn attacks against Saudi Arabia and reaffirm our commitment to the Kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, and security.” He stressed that Pakistan remained supportive of any meaningful diplomatic engagement that could contribute to “ending hostilities and achieving a durable political settlement”. Earlier this month, the FO said that Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye had agreed to deploy military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom, following an emergency meeting of the SPDC formed under their joint defence agreement in Riyadh. While the statement did not specifically name any threat, the development came against the backdrop of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in the Yemen conflict. The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait in a lightning offensive in September.

title: R4 bloc, European powers discuss developments in the Gulf in Istanbul meeting
description: Developments in the Gulf region amid the US-Israeli war on Iran came under discussion as the R4 foreign ministers — Pakistan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye — met with their counterparts from France, Germany, Italy and the United Kingdom. The R4 group, comprising Pakistan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, emerged in March and has been focusing on regional security and mediation efforts between the United States and Iran. According to the Foreign Office (FO), Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar participated in the first meeting between the R4 and France, Germany, Italy and the UK. “The meeting provided an opportunity for exchange of views on regional developments in the Gulf region, their social and economic impacts, and the urgent need to foster diplomatic engagement to resolve regional challenges of peace, security and stability,” it said. “Dar briefed his counterparts on the diplomatic and mediatory role Pakistan continues to play in de-escalating tensions, preventing resumption of hostilities and promoting peace. All ministers agreed for continued engagement in this format,” it said. The R4 bloc also held a separate meeting. According to the FO, Dar participated in the sixth R4 foreign ministers’ meeting alongside Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, and Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud of Saudi Arabia. The ministers reviewed developments in the region since their last meeting in New York in September, with “particular focus on the situation in the Middle East and related security challenges and conflicts”, the FO said. They expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed their support for its sovereignty and territorial integrity. The FO added that the ministers also condemned the Houthi attacks targeting Saudi Arabia and underscored the importance of respecting state sovereignty. “They discussed ways to strengthen regional coordination and advance diplomatic efforts to promote lasting peace, security, and stability,” it said. A joint statement issued after the meeting detailed that the ministers particularly condemned Houthi strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, as well as attacks carried out against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab. “They expressed their full solidarity with the government of Yemen and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and called on the Houthi militia to immediately cease all military actions, threats and attacks, and to return to the political process in good faith,” the statement said. Regarding the US-Iran conflict and the Strait of Hormuz, they stressed the “urgent need” to address this conflict only through dialogue and diplomacy, as well as to prevent the targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructures, including vessels. They expressed support for the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and welcomed continued diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation and reaffirmed their commitment to a lasting negotiated solution, the joint statement said. The participants further underscored the “vital importance” of freedom of navigation, permanent maritime safety and security and safeguarding navigational rights and freedoms. “They noted that disruption of sea lanes threatens the security and prosperity of all, through blocking global supply chains, flows of energy, fertiliser and food, impacting vulnerable populations in the region and beyond, and thus, requires collective efforts by the international community to address these challenges.” The ministers also rejected any measures or restrictions that impair lawful navigation and called for the swift and full resumption of safe, secure and unimpeded passage through the Strait of Hormuz, the statement said, adding that the participants agreed to maintain close consultation and coordination on the afore-mentioned matters. Moreover, they emphasised that the Israeli occupation in Gaza constituted the “fundamental source of instability” in the region and beyond, and that Israeli policies creates a “deep sense of injustice in global public opinion”. They called for the early implementation of the two-state solution in Palestine, in accordance with the relevant UN resolutions. “They reiterated their support for the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people, including their inalienable right to self-determination and to establish an independent, sovereign, viable, and contiguous State of Palestine on the basis of the 4 June 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital, in accordance with relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions in order to achieve comprehensive peace in the Middle East,” the statement said. The ministers called for an “urgent end” to the ongoing Israeli violence, as well as attempts to change the legal and historical status of Jerusalem, and to bring an end to further destruction and humanitarian tragedy in Palestine. They condemned all the previous and current settlement activities in the West Bank and Jerusalem, as well as the settler violence against Palestinians and underlined the urgent need for uninterrupted flow of humanitarian aid to and reconstruction in Gaza. Bilateral meetings Dar earlier held bilateral meetings with the Turkish and Egyptian foreign ministers, on the sidelines of the R4 meeting and a meeting between the R4 and European diplomats in Istanbul, the FO said. In a post on X, the FO said that Dar met with Fidan ahead of the ministerial meeting, thanking him for hosting the meetings. The pair discussed bilateral relations and regional developments, particularly the situation in the Middle East and Palestine. “They expressed concern over threats to regional stability and underscored the importance of dialogue, diplomacy and coordinated efforts to promote regional peace and security,” the FO statement said. Additionally, Dar and Fidan strongly condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed their commitment to close coordination on regional issues, including under the Makkah Defence Agreement. “Both leaders reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening the longstanding bonds of friendship and brotherhood between Pakistan and Turkiye, and to deepening cooperation across all areas of mutual interest, both bilaterally and in multilateral fora,” the FO added. Later, the FO said that Dar also met with Egyptian FM Abdelatty on the sidelines of the ministerial meeting, where the two exchanged views on regional and international developments. In particular, they discussed the situation in Palestine and the Middle East, and underscored the importance of “sustained dialogue and diplomacy” in addressing challenges in the region. The two reaffirmed the “longstanding and fraternal ties” between Pakistan and Egypt, and highlighted the importance of sustained high-level engagement to further advance bilateral relations, the FO statement said. “They agreed to impart greater momentum to cooperation across a range of areas, including trade, business-to-business linkages, agriculture, pharmaceutical, connectivity, renewable energy, defence, and people-to-people exchanges,” the FO added. The ministers also reaffirmed their commitment to continued consultations and closer coordination under the R4 framework, as well as on matters of mutual interest, it said. The deputy premier later had a “warm and cordial meeting” with Saudi FM Prince Faisal bin Farhan, where he expressed Pakistan’s full support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the kingdom. “The two leaders reaffirmed the enduring strength of the fraternal ties between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia and their commitment to further strengthening their strategic partnership through close cooperation across all areas of interest and regular consultations at all levels,” the FO said. They also underscored the “special bond” between their countries, reinforced by their bilateral Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement and the Makkah defence agreement between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia; as well as their shared commitment to regional peace, security and stability, it added. Separately, DPM Dar met with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on the sidelines of the meeting and expressed the desire to further strengthen bilateral ties “through sustained engagement and cooperation across multiple areas of mutual interest”, the FO said. According to the FO, the two ministers discussed relations between Pakistan and Germany and exchanged views on regional and international developments. They stressed the importance of dialogue, diplomacy and sustained international engagement to promote peace and stability and to address the evolving challenges in the region. Dar “welcomed the constructive engagement” of Germany, France, Italy and the UK with the R4 framework, the FO said, adding that he underscored the value of “continued consultations and diplomatic coordination on issues of shared concern”. Talks to revolve around Hormuz, Saudi Arabia British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband’s office said the talks would essentially revolve around “the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia”. It said Miliband “will advocate for a diplomatic solution to the [Hormuz] crisis that restores full navigational rights and freedoms”. He will also stress “how Iranian tactics are being replicated across the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilising the region and increasing pressure on vital waterways and global chokepoints, such as Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal”, it added. France confirmed the talks on “the Iranian crisis in its various ramifications”, hailing it as a first “in this format … against a backdrop of extreme instability and uncertainty in the region.” The meeting will aim to “strengthen coordination between Europeans and Middle Eastern countries in the face of crises that we did not choose and that affect us all,” the French foreign ministry said. Fidan is expected to emphasise the need for a diplomatic solution to the war between the United States and Iran, the importance of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, and reiterate Turkiye’s support for Saudi Arabia’s security against attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels under the Makkah defence agreement signed by Islamabad, Ankara, and Riyadh, the sources said. The Makkah defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.

title: German president meets Zardari, praises Pakistan's 'rising diplomatic profile' in dispute resolution
description: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier praised Pakistan’s “rising diplomatic profile in the resolution of regional and global disputes”, in a meeting with President Asif Ali Zardari in Berlin on Friday. President Zardari is currently on a three-day visit to Germany, having departed yesterday, as the two countries are set to mark the 75th anniversary of their diplomatic relations. According to a statement posted by the president’s office, the two leaders also discussed challenges related to Afghanistan. President Zardari said that while Pakistan “has no conflict with the Afghan people”, it would not allow terrorists to use Afghan soil to attack Pakistan’s citizens and violate its sovereignty. Steinmeier appreciated Pakistan for facilitating the verification of 500 Afghans “destined to be repatriated to Germany”, it said, adding that he also commended Pakistan’s humanitarian assistance to “millions of Afghans” over more than four decades. He also took a “significant interest” in the Makkah defence pact, which has been signed between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia. In response, President Zardari said the pact was aimed at “ensuring regional security and provided a security alternative to regional conflicts, and it is not directed against any specific country”. The German president expressed hope that the two countries would continue to engage with reinforced efforts in the fields of business and trade to promote “bilateral business, education collaboration and technological cooperation”. For his part, President Zardari thanked Steinmeier for his invitation and the hospitality extended to him and his delegation. President Zardari further expressed his gratitude for Steinmeier’s acknowledgement of Pakistan’s “sincere mediation role” in the conflict between the United States and Iran, the statement said. He said Pakistan viewed the resolution of conflicts through the lens of sustained dialogue and constructive negotiations, “for the sake of regional as well as global peace and stability”. During the meeting, President Zardari also stressed the need to “realise the available potential for expanding existing political, economic and defence cooperation” between Pakistan and Germany, with “greater focus on economy and trade, emerging technologies, climate resilience, skills development, people-to-people and cultural exchanges”, the statement said. The president said that Pakistan “highly values” Germany as a major European partner, and expressed admiration for German support towards women’s empowerment, social protection and human development. Pakistan was prepared for expanding bilateral cooperation beyond traditional areas into “innovative and mutually beneficial collaboration” with Germany, in the areas of scientific development, healthcare and education, vocational training and technological advancement, trade and investment, agriculture, commerce and industry, and climate resilience, through enhanced government-to-government, business-to-business and expert-level interactions, the statement further quoted President Zardari as saying. He said the visit reflected Pakistan’s “commitment to deepening its longstanding cordial, friendly relations with Germany and readiness to translate existing relations into a stronger, robust and mutually beneficial partnership through sustained constructive engagement”. President Zardari invited the German president to Pakistan, who responded that he would consider a visit “at an appropriate time”. Both presidents participated in delegation-level talks after their one-on-one meeting, according to the statement. Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah and Sindh’s provincial ministers Sharjeel Memon and Jam Khan Shoro, Senator Saleem Mandviwalla and Pakistan’s Ambassador to Germany Salman Sharif were part of the Pakistani delegation. Earlier, President Zardari was given a guard of honour upon his arrival at the German Ministry of Defence, with Steinmeier also present on the occasion, the statement added. In a statement issued on Thursday, the Foreign Office (FO) said the president’s visit, scheduled for Oct 22-24, is “part of high-level exchanges between Pakistan and Germany”. During his visit, he will also hold meetings with senior leadership and business leaders, with a “particular focus on economic and trade cooperation”, the FO said. In September, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. During the meeting, Germany appreciated Pakistan’s mediation efforts in regional conflicts, especially in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab. The two sides also agreed to “get negotiations on peace for Ukraine going”, according to the German foreign office. In June, a German delegation announced plans to bring about 30 German companies to Pakistan and link local businesses to European markets.

title: 'Will petrol be available in December?': Senate echoes with shortage concerns even as state minister says no supply issues
description: ISLAMABAD: The Senate echoed with fuel supply concerns on Friday as PPP’s Sherry Rehman questioned petrol availability for December and Opposition Leader Raja Nasir Abbas warned of a bleak situation amid heightening Middle East tensions. The concerns were raised even after Minister of State for Finance and Revenue Bilal Azhar Kayani said that there were no supply issues. He told the Senate during the question hour that more than 10 million people were benefiting from the government’s targeted fuel subsidy scheme, while Rs1,676 billion had been budgeted under the petroleum levy for the current year. The subsidy was being provided at petrol pumps, and there was no fuel supply problem, he said. Kayani added that the impact of regional conflict on petroleum prices was being felt across countries, but the government was providing targeted relief to motorcyclists, rickshaw and loader operators, and users of small cars. Last week, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb also said Pakistan had enough supplies to last through November. But what about December? asked PPP’s Rehman in the Senate on Friday. “What is the government’s plan for the availability of petroleum products? Will there be rationing? Members of Parliament have concerns whether petrol will be available till December,” she said. She demanded that the government brief Parliament on any rationing and contingency plans it may have been working on. Senator Rehman said reports of renewed attacks on Iran and escalating conflict in West Asia had added to uncertainty surrounding Pakistan’s petroleum supplies and had direct implications for the country’s energy security, economic stability and lives of ordinary citizens. Wondering if Pakistan would have adequate supplies under current circumstances, she said, “These are not minor concerns.” She warned that any disruption in the supply of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) would have a serious impact across the country, pointing out that Pakistan relied on imports for nearly 70 per cent of its LPG requirements while domestic production accounted for only 30pc. Pakistan received five LPG cargoes last year, whereas only two were expected this year, she said, demanding that a supply plan be presented to Parliament. Turning to the carbon levy, the PPP senator, who chairs the Senate Standing Committee on Climate Change, claimed the carbon levy on petroleum products was not being spent on environmental protection. “Yesterday, during the meeting of the Senate Standing Committee on Climate Change, the finance additional secretary acknowledged that the carbon levy is not being spent on environmental projects. A levy is not a tax; it goes straight into the Federal Consolidated Fund where there is no ring-fencing for spending on climate action,” she said. Rehman added that the revelation confirmed what was denied earlier during a Senate session. “The levy is being absorbed into general federal receipts instead of being earmarked for climate resilience despite severe and devastating floods facing all provinces,” she alleged. “The federal government continues to collect this revenue through the petroleum levy, and the money goes into the Federal Consolidated Fund; it cuts through all the provinces. There should not be a carbon levy in the next budget, unless it is restructured as a carbon tax that is ring-fenced for mitigation and climate action. There has to be accountability for every rupee collected.” “When an item is called a carbon levy, it is to be ring-fenced and then disbursed in consultation with the climate ministry,” she asserted. For his part, Senate Opposition Leader Raja Nasir Abbas warned that a war engulfing key energy routes would worsen Pakistan’s energy crisis, as key maritime chokepoints come under threat. He linked the external crisis to domestic shortages, saying Punjab was already facing a flour shortage while the country was witnessing an LPG shortage. Meanwhile, politicians were ignoring real issues and were busy trying to “ conquer ” provinces, he said, seemingly referring to the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Oct 11. He also questioned the claims that terrorists were given shelter in Swat and asked how many had been caught. Meanwhile, police, who were the guarantors of peace, were being made to fight the public, he claimed. He also touched upon the conflict between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia, saying that Pakistan should mediate between the two sides. With Yemen’s civil war flaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attacked Saudi infrastructure , including energy facilities and airports, in recent days. This, coupled with the US-Israeli war on Iran that began in February, has resulted in the choking of key energy supply routes — the Straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and energy price hikes globally. Finance Minister Aurangzeb said during an interview last week that Pakistan had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices, but attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were “worrying” for the country’s longer-term economic outlook. He said the country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.

title: NCCIA prevents Karachi girl exposed to dark web group from causing self-harm: official
description: KARACHI: The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) prevented a teenage girl in Karachi from causing self-harm after she was influenced by a group operating on the dark web, an official told Dawn on Friday. NCCIA Karachi Additional Director Tariq Nawaz said action by the agency was taken after they received a lead from a foreign crime investigation agency, which he did not name. The agency also shared an email, he said, adding that the NCCIA then tracked the relevant user internet protocol (IP) address. The official separately explained while speaking on Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ that information had been shared with the NCCIA that a group operating on the dark web had been influencing people to commit violent acts. He added that once the NCCIA was able to track down the affected girl, it transpired during a probe that she had been exposed to the group through social media. “She then engaged with them on a messaging application and was being assigned different tasks.” Nawaz said the tasks also included harming her pet, and the NCCIA was able to trace her before she could complete the next task, which was causing self-harm. He also said the devices in the girl’s use had been analysed and taken into custody for further examination. Speaking to Dawn , the official said the girl’s parents told the NCCIA that their daughter’s behaviour had changed over the past three or four months; she remained upset but did not divulge anything when the parents insisted that she share some information as to whether she was facing problems. Nawaz said an investigation was ongoing and the NCCIA was working to ascertain other possible victims and perpetrators involved in similar activities. The NCCIA official said “psychological counselling” had been provided to the girl to help her recover from “trauma”. The NCCIA had received another tip-off from a foreign agency earlier this month in another case involving a teenager, who was sent to jail on judicial remand for allegedly attempting to poison his father after seeking help from artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots. The suspect, who was inspired by an OTT crime series, allegedly procured chemical substances from Australia and Islamabad and even set up a small laboratory at his house to prepare the poison. The boy allegedly also used AI tools and online platforms to seek information regarding poisonous chemicals and discussed ways to poison his father with AI bots. On receiving a tip-off from a US agency, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the NCCIA conducted a raid at the suspect’s house and arrested him on Sept 23.

title: Lahore DC gives formal go-ahead for 3-day Basant festivities in March 2027, outlines conditions and restrictions
description: LAHORE: The Lahore deputy commissioner (DC) on Friday gave the formal go-ahead for three-day Basant festivities in the district from March 12-14 next year, outlining guidelines, conditions and restrictions for the celebrations. Basant returned to Lahore earlier this year after an 18-year hiatus, with the passing of the Punjab Regulation of Kite Flying Bill, 2025 by the provincial assembly on December 24, 2025. The legislation authorised deputy commissioners to grant conditional permission for kite-flying — which otherwise remains banned in Punjab — on specified days and at designated locations. In August, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz announced that the festival would next be celebrated from March 12-14. On Friday, the decision was formalised in notification by the Lahore DC. The notification, a copy of which is available with Dawn , said that kite-flying would be allowed in Lahore during Basant 2027 except at designated prohibited zones and subject to certain conditions. “Kite-flying through the use of permissible kite-flying material, as specified in Schedule-I of the Punjab Regulation of Kite Flying Rules, 2025 and Punjab Kite Flying Regulations, 2025 shall be allowed from March 12-14, 2027,” it added. The notification said the manufacturing of permissible kite-flying material would be allowed from Sept 5, 2026 to March 14, 2027, subject to valid digital registration. Trade, including the purchase, transportation and storage of the material, will be permitted from Feb 1, 2027 to March 14, 2027 while sales to the general public will be allowed from Feb 10, 2027 to March 14, 2027, exclusively through registered sellers. The notification further said that no manufacturer, trader, or seller should manufacture, trade, store or sell permissible kite-flying material unless registered with the deputy commissioner through the government’s eBiz application. “ Patang (kite) shall not exceed four-and-a-half githi (span of a hand) and 35 inches in width and 30 inches in length,” it said. “ Gudda (a large kite) shall not exceed one-and-a-half tawa and 40 inches in width and 34 inches in length,” the notification added. The kite string, known as dor , shall only be wound in the shape of pinna , it must be made of cotton with no more than nine taars (threads) and no fewer than 28 counts and shall be coated with maanjha having a minimum sheesha size of 350 mesh. “Preparation, coating, treatment or processing of dor or maanjha shall be strictly restricted to maya (laundry starch), 350-mesh glass powder and only rice flour, and no other material, chemical, adhesive, hardener, abrasive, metallic substance or strengthening agent, including rema tip top, amri powder or any other material having similar properties or effect, whether used individually or in combination with the permitted material shall be added, mixed or applied at any stage,” the notification said. The DC also prohibited the manufacture, trading, transportation, storage, sale, possession and use of charkhi , sharp maanjha , metallic wire, nylon (plastic) dandi , and any other thread coated with sharp maanjha or any other injurious material. Registered manufacturers, traders and sellers will be required to “conspicuously” display their valid registration certificates at approved premises for kite-flying. “Complete stock, sales and movement records shall be maintained and produced on demand by registered manufacturers, traders and sellers to any authorised officer of the deputy commissioner.” The notification further said that all registered kite-flying associations should comply with the functions assigned under the Punjab Regulation of Kite Flying Rules, 2025 and remain in close coordination with the deputy commissioner and his authorised officers for smooth and safe conduct of kite-flying. Moreover, motorcyclists in Lahore would be required to comply with all the safety measures, including the installation of safety rods, as specified in Chapter-III of the Punjab Kite Flying Regulations 2025 and guidelines issued by the Punjab government secretary and the Home Department under the kite flying law. “All departments, attached departments, agencies and government organisations shall assist the district administration and police for strict compliance of [the] terms and conditions to ensure public safety,” the notification said. According to the notification, kite-flying will not be permitted in the following areas of Lahore during Basant: Aircraft approach path Nadirabad Gulshan Ali Colony Nishat Colony Bhatta Chowk DHA Lahore (blocks R, S, P and Q) Aircraft take-off path Al-Faisal Town Jorraypul Canal Bank Road (adjacent to tajoura) Tajpura Basant had been banned in 2007 because of an increasing number of deaths and serious injuries caused by sharp strings, particularly to motorcyclists and pillion riders, as well as by celebratory gunfire. It was allowed to be celebrated for the first time since then earlier this year, but only in Lahore.

title: AIPAC’s shift
description: ON Wednesday, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) made an unusual announcement . The organisation would no longer endorse or make direct contributions to candidates running in US elections. This marks the end of a practice that AIPAC began in 2021 (its lobbying started in the ‘50s). This does not mean that the Israel lobby will stop trying to influence US elections. AIPAC will continue mobilising individual donors. However, the announcement is an acknowledgement of the growing difficulties associated with overt affiliation with the lobby and the pro-Israel agenda. The genocide in Gaza and the war in Iran have created a situation where many Americans are questioning their country’s support for Israel and the resources devoted to it. Democratic candidates have challenged US involvement in the Middle East and the $3.8 billion in annual assistance Washington provides Israel. No campaign has illustrated this with greater clarity than that of Dr Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the US Senate seat in Michigan. In the Democratic primary, AIPAC spent $30 million backing El-Sayed’s opponent, Haley Stevens. Other political action committees also spent heavily on her campaign. In contrast, El-Sayed spent only $3.2m, most of it raised from individual donors. Despite all this, El-Sayed won. One reason was his willingness to confront Stevens over AIPAC’s involvement in the race and to question why US taxpayer money should go to another country. What El-Sayed was able to do is connect two different realities of the American political context. First, he tapped into the American fatigue with interminable wars in the Middle East. Again, and again, he argued that the US had “no business” becoming embroiled in further conflicts, while infrastructure and institutions at home were decaying. His criticism of Donald Trump’s escapades in Iran became part of this argument. Second, El-Sayed connected the affordability crisis facing Americans to questions about government spending and the country’s relationship with Israel. Americans struggling to afford healthcare and basic groceries are naturally questioning how public money is spent abroad. War-weary Americans can see through Israeli machinations. El-Sayed is not campaigning on Israel alone. Affordability and healthcare are central issues for him, and he supports a government-funded Medicare For All option that would make healthcare accessible to millions of people. His own background in public health makes him a persuasive speaker on these issues. AIPAC’s affiliated Super PAC has now directed spending against El-Sayed in his contest with Republican Mike Rogers. This is a departure from AIPAC’s usual support for Democratic candidates in Michigan. American Zionists and the well-heeled donors behind AIPAC may see the Michigan contest not simply as an electoral battle in a US state but also as an indicator of how anti-Israel sentiment is becoming increasingly pervasive among the Democratic electorate. The announcement that there will be no more overt endorsements reflects the liability that public association with AIPAC can create for some candidates. It is a sea change in the character of Democratic politics in the US. There are global implications in this shift. If El-Sayed wins — and one hopes he does despite the millions that AIPAC is now pouring into his opponent’s coffers — it will mean that other Democratic lawmakers in the House and Senate will have to think twice about voting to send billions of dollars to Israel. In the past, Democratic politicians have voted en masse for just these sorts of measures. Israel is very proud of its genocidal actions in Gaza. It is also quite smug about having persua­d­­ed Trump to at­­tack Iran. It sees both of these act­ions and its continuing excesses in Gaza and the West Bank as victories. This, however, is an illusion. The reality is that in the process of achieving the former, Israelis forgot that ordinary, war-weary Americans can see through its machinations. This is important not because Israel cares what Americans think but because Israel is entirely dependent on the US, receiving almost 70 per cent of its military equipment from them. As the election of Zohran Mamdani in New York City and the hopeful rise of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan show, Americans are signalling just how fed up they are with Israel’s intrusions in their own government and its attempts to create dual loyalties in their political leadership. As American leaders stop signing blank cheques for Israel as in the past five decades, Israel is likely to face enormous struggles. Already an isolated nation, increasingly detested by the world for the carnage of innocents, its future is not that of a victorious nation but of a widely reviled one. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy. rafia.zakaria@gmail.com Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: Beyond tariff cuts
description: PAKISTAN cannot build a competitive industry by protecting it indefinitely. Nor can reducing protection, by itself, turn domestic manufacturers into exporters. Tariffs shape investment decisi­o­­ns, but competitiveness also depends on energy, te­­­chnology, scale, supply chains, market access, and security. A credible industrial strategy must address them together. Unconditional protection raises prices, blunts incentives to innovate, and rewards selling to a captive home market. Consu­mers finance inefficiency, and capital chases protected returns rather than export opportunities. Where there is no credible prospect of competitiveness, protection merely postpones adjustment at public expense. The National Tariff Policy 2025-30 , therefore, points broadly in the right direction. Fewer tariff slabs, cheaper imported inputs, and phased elimination of additional customs and regulatory duties can lower costs and reduce the bias against exports. But these are instruments of competitiveness, not substitutes for the conditions that make exports possible. The essential complement is a measurable programme to cut the costs the state imposes on production. If manufacturers face a timetable for lower protection, the government should face one for affordable, reliable energy, prompt tax refunds, simpler regulation, and efficient logistics. Otherwise, industry is asked to adjust while the state’s own contribution to uncompetitiveness goes unaddressed. This is not an argument for waiting until every domestic problem is solved; that would make protection permanent. It is a case for distinguishing activities with little prospect of competitiveness, those capable of achieving it, and a narrow set of strategic capabilities. The polyester chain shows the cost of failing to draw these distinctions. The textile industry association, APTMA, argues that protection on polyester staple fibre and its key input, purified terephthalic acid, raises costs for downstream textiles, while the country’s sole PTA plant, commissioned in 1998, lags newer plants in China and India. These claims by interested users warrant independent examination. The test is straightforward. Has prolonged support delivered globally competitive costs, technological upgrading, and lower energy use per tonne? Has it helped downstream producers compete in synthetic and blended textiles? Protection that preserves an inefficient input supplier while handicapping a much larger export opportunity defeats its own purpose. Energy illustrates the shared responsibility. High electricity tariffs and excessive electricity consumption are different problems: the government must fix the first; manufacturers must invest to reduce the second. Consumers and downstream exporters should not indefinitely finance either failure. Protection that preserves an inefficient input supplier while handicapping a much larger export opportunity defeats its own purpose. Yet an equally indiscriminate withdrawal of support could destroy capabilities with a viable future. Auto parts deserve assessment on this basis. Complaints about expensive vehicles and meagre exports obscure engineering skills within the supplier base. Toolmaking, casting, machining, moulding, process control, and quality assurance are not tied to one vehicle. Partnerships with foreign manufacturers can develop capabilities serving replacement markets, other engineering industries, and, where specifications permit, defence production. These capabilities justify scrutiny and selective development, not permanent protection for every assembler or component. The right unit of assessment is often the product or process, not the entire sector. Scale is crucial. Investment in moulds, testing or automated lines must be recovered over sufficient output; short runs make each unit expensive. Too many models fragment demand in a small market, while differing specifications prevent vendors from supplying the same part to several assemblers. Policy should encourage viable specialisation, common components where feasible, supplier consolidation, and access to replacement and export markets. A vendor serving several customers can reach volumes that no single low-volume model offers. Competition policy must accompany consolidation, so that scale raises productivity rather than market power. Upstream supply matters too. Reliable access to automotive-grade steel, engineering plastics and specialised chemicals affects quality, cost, lead times, and working capital. A competitive local supplier can shorten delivery and support joint development, but domestic steel or petrochemical production alone guarantees neither. Pakistan need not make every input before it can export. Where domestic production lacks scale or technology, predictable access to competitively priced imports is essential; forcing manufacturers to buy costly local inputs shifts protection upstream and erodes downstream competitiveness. The goal is an efficient supply chain combining viable domestic capabilities with dependable imports, not local-content targets. Market access is the next missing piece. Cutting Pakistan’s import tariffs does nothing to lower the duties its exporters face abroad. Preferential trade agreements can open larger markets, but their value depends on product coverage, rules of origin, and real commercial opportunities. They should be negotiated around what Pakistan can competitively supply and what investors could realistically produce. Buyers also weigh security. Export relationships depend on plant visits, technical assistance, audits, and dependable delivery. Insecurity, transport disruptions or barriers to foreign experts can cancel out a competitive price. Buyers pay for reliability, and investors need confidence that people, equipment and goods can travel safely. How, then, should protection be withdrawn? Activities with no credible route to competitiveness should have a clear exit timetable. Those with demonstrable potential should receive temporary support tied to investment, productivity, quality, energy efficiency, and a narrowing price gap with imports. Government should accept published obligations on costs and business conditions. An independent review should distinguish policy failures from outdated equipment, inadequate scale, or poor management. Verified government failures could justify limited adjustments to the tariff timetable, each with a firm expiry. Industry must not gain a permanent veto over reform. Strategic exceptions should remain narrow. Food security can justify agricultural resilience without self-sufficiency in every crop. Defence can justify selected domestic capabilities despite higher costs, subject to periodic review of their security value and expense. Lower tariffs on inputs remove one obstacle to exports. They cannot supply scale, modern technology, efficiency, market access, or security. Pakistan needs a reciprocal bargain: industry must earn support through performance, and the government must deliver conditions for competition. Neither should hand consumers an indefinite bill for its failures. The writeris a former CEO of Unilever Pakistan and of the Pakistan Business Council. Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: Breaking the cycle
description: THE World Bank’s latest Pakistan Development Update sets out what faster reforms could deliver for the economy. If policies and institutions matched those of an average middle-income country, it estimates, annual growth could reach 6.2-6.9pc , enough to reach Vietnam’s current income level, and incomes would triple by 2050. The distance from here is long. Real GDP growth rose to 3.65pc in FY26 and the primary surplus reached 2.9pc of GDP. But per capita income is currently growing at only about 1.6pc, which means the economy has been put in better financial order without making most people better off. The country’s return to macroeconomic stability is widely appreciated by international lenders and credit agencies. However, it is not the same thing as a solid foundation for rapid growth. Much of this stability has come from holding the economy down. High interest rates, fiscal tightening, and costly energy have dampened demand and squeezed imports, easing pressure on the external account. Workers’ remittances have helped the current account and rebuilt reserves, and continued external borrowing has bought time. But none of this builds capacity. Borrowing defers the bill, remittances bring in dollars without adding to domestic output, and compressed imports can fix the external balance while leaving exports no more competitive. The stability that results depends on inflows continuing and on the government keeping up its restraint. That is why any real push for growth can be risky. It would mean more imported machinery, fuel, industrial inputs, and consumer goods. If exports and productivity do not keep pace, the current account slips, reserves fall, and policymakers enforce tightening again. We have been through this cycle many times. Breaking it means changing what the economy produces and sells, not just how fast it is allowed to grow. The obstacles are well known: unreliable and costly energy, a narrow tax base, cumbersome regulation, weak competition, and a poorly skilled workforce. Policy keeps changing, which deters long-term investment. Tax reform must bring undertaxed sectors into the net, instead of increasing the burden on those already compliant. Energy reform has to cut system costs rather than shift them between consumers and the budget. And exports need a policy that works beyond incentives. Macroeconomic stability cannot carry the economy much further without better productivity. The World Bank’s numbers are best read as a reform target. Reaching Vietnam’s income level will take sustained spending on education, health, infrastructure, and technology, and institutions that can be trusted. It will also take growth that creates more than just better headline figures. If the government does not use the present breathing space to raise productivity, boost exports, and complete lasting energy and tax reforms, the next growth push could bring back the crisis Pakistan has just come out of. Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: UK tells public to keep 3 days' emergency supplies at home following PHP software glitch
description: The British government advised the public on Friday to keep three days of emergency supplies at home, a message it said had been hammered home by this week’s PHP software glitch , as well as a record-setting summer of heat, drought and wildfires. Governments and businesses worldwide have rushed to secure systems running the PHP programming language after flaws were disclosed on Wednesday, forcing some services offline and triggering millions of hacking attempts in one of the most significant cybersecurity incidents in recent years. The British government said the internet outage showed the importance of its newly launched “Be Ready” campaign, which advises the public to keep three days of bottled water and non-perishable food in the house. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, hosting a meeting on the response to wildfires, said that in the past Britain had been “on the back foot” responding to emergencies and that it needed to be more proactive. The government announced a new wildfire response plan that includes deploying military aircraft. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said cyber incidents such as the PHP outage would become more common as AI made it easier to find ways to thwart traditional defences. He also cited risks from hostile states, organised criminals and climate change. The UK was facing a greater level of threat “than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime”, he said during an appearance on the BBC’s ‘Question Time’ programme broadcast overnight. Britain’s advice is similar to that issued by the European Commission, which told EU citizens last year to keep a 72-hour emergency kit containing supplies such as food, water, cash and power banks.

title: Hasan Nawaz is finding his feet, and Pakistan could reap the rewards
description: Pakistan have spent much of the past few years searching for stability in their middle order. The problem has been particularly pronounced at number six, where the ability to rebuild an innings must go hand in hand with the capacity to accelerate at short notice. Finding a batter who can do both has proved easier said than done. Hasan Nawaz may yet provide an answer. At 81-4, with Pakistan needing to recover from a precarious position during their One-day International tri-series match on Tuesday, few batters would have dared to launch Adil Rashid for a first-ball six. Hasan did just that. It was a reminder of the natural power and confidence that have made him an exciting prospect, even as questions over his consistency continue to follow him. His international career, so far, has been a study in contrasts. In only his third Twenty20 International (T20I), Hasan smashed an unbeaten 105 off 45 balls to help Pakistan chase down 205 in Auckland. It was a statement innings from a batter who appeared to have the game to succeed at the highest level. Yet his other four innings at the start of his international career yielded just one run between them. The promise was unmistakable, but so was the inconsistency. The contrast between his best and worst returns illustrates the challenge Pakistan have faced in getting the best out of Hasan. The talent was evident, but converting those flashes of brilliance into a sustained run of performances remained a work in progress. A productive stint in the Pakistan Super League (PSL) followed, with Hasan rediscovering his touch at number four. The team management subsequently tried him in the middle order, but the returns were patchy. A string of low scores towards the end of 2025 eventually cost him his place in the T20I side. There were, however, encouraging signs in the 50-over format. Hasan made his One-Day International (ODI) debut in October 2025 and announced himself with an unbeaten 63 off 54 balls against the West Indies, earning the player-of-the-match award. Coming in with Pakistan at 180-5 in pursuit of 285 on a tricky surface, he showed both skill and temperament to guide the chase. He followed that effort with unbeaten scores of 36 and 13, finishing the tour with 113 runs at an average of 56.5. Despite that promising start, his T20I struggles continued, and he was sidelined after playing just one ODI against South Africa in November 2025. In hindsight, Pakistan might have benefited from giving him a longer run in ODIs. At the time, however, the decision was understandable. Hasan appeared to have lost his way, and a spell away from international cricket seemed a reasonable opportunity to rebuild his game. That process was far from straightforward. During the 2025-26 International League T20 (ILT20), Hasan managed just 124 runs in 10 innings, largely in a role that required him to slog at the death. The problem was not his ability to clear the boundary; it was his capacity to build an innings before unleashing that power. By then, he had acquired the familiar reputation of a batter who could be devastating on his day but was just as capable of going missing. A subsequent stint with Sialkot in the National T20 Cup provided a turning point. Rather than relying on his power from the outset, Hasan began to rethink how he approached an innings. His six-hitting ability was never in doubt. What needed work was the route he took to get there. The shift was prompted in part by Sialkot head coach Naveed Latif, who advised him to start more cautiously and make up for lost time later in the innings. Hasan took the advice to heart. He finished the tournament as the second-highest run-scorer, striking at an impressive 155. His most striking performance came against Multan in a virtual quarter-final. At one stage, he had managed only a run-a-ball 21, but then he exploded, scoring 59 off his next 19 deliveries to finish unbeaten on 80 off 40. It was an extraordinary turnaround, and a demonstration of what Hasan could achieve when he married patience with power. For a batter who had struggled to reconcile the two, it was an encouraging sign that his game was beginning to take shape. His returns in the last season of the Pakistan Super League were respectable, if hardly spectacular. The adjustment was not without its drawbacks: Hasan could spend too long settling in and then find himself unable to accelerate when the pressure mounted. The approach that had worked in domestic cricket was not necessarily a formula he could replicate at international level. That distinction matters. T20 cricket offers little room for a batter to recover from a slow start, particularly when the required rate is climbing. Whether Hasan’s new approach will consistently work in T20Is remains an open question, and the sample size since his return is too small to draw firm conclusions. There have, nevertheless, been glimpses of its potential. Against India at the Asian Games, he scored 96 off 51 balls after initially struggling to get going, reaching six off his first 11 deliveries. India’s sloppy fielding helped his cause, but Hasan deserves credit for capitalising on the opportunities and accelerating when it mattered. In the recently concluded T20I series against Sri Lanka, he struck an important unbeaten 19 off nine balls in the second match, providing a late boost to the innings. His scratchy 17 off 16 in the third, however, offered a reminder that the method is far from foolproof. A slow start can provide a platform for acceleration, but it can just as easily leave a batter with too much to do in too little time. For now, Hasan seems willing to take that risk. The challenge is to recognise when the situation demands patience and when it requires him to attack from the outset. It is in ODIs, though, that Hasan’s development could prove particularly valuable to Pakistan. For the last couple of years, Salman Ali Agha has been a dependable presence in the middle order, batting primarily at number five. The position below him has been far less settled. Pakistan have tried several options at number six, with little sustained success, and the search for a reliable finisher who can also rebuild an innings has continued. Salman has occasionally batted at number six, but with him expected to occupy the number five position heading into the World Cup, it makes more sense to assess the alternatives. The chart below illustrates Pakistan’s returns at number six, excluding Salman. Batting at number six is among the more demanding jobs in white-ball cricket. A batter may have to rescue an innings after a collapse, rotate the strike while wickets are falling, or walk in with only a handful of overs remaining and be expected to score quickly. There is rarely much time to settle in, and the demands can change from one match to the next. It is also an unforgiving role. A 20-ball 35 might barely register, while a failure to score quickly enough or a dismissal during a rebuild can attract scrutiny. The ideal number six must be adaptable enough to manage both situations, and Pakistan have struggled to find someone who can do so consistently. Hasan’s recent ODI performances suggest he could be worth backing in that role. Earlier this year, he scored two half-centuries in three outings for his team in the National Champions Cup while batting at number five. His return to the ODI side has been equally encouraging, highlighted by a 79 off 74 balls against England earlier this week. The innings was significant not merely for the runs it produced, but for the way Hasan appeared to learn from his recent struggles. In the opening match of the tri-series, against Sri Lanka, he had found it difficult to rotate the strike, reaching 22 not out off 40 balls at one stage before managing a few boundaries and eventually falling for 37 off 49. It was an awkward innings, and one that raised questions about whether his cautious approach was becoming counterproductive. Against England, the response was immediate. Hasan produced a fluent half-century off 46 balls, showing greater intent and a better grasp of when to attack. The contrast between the two innings was encouraging: he had identified a weakness and appeared to address it without abandoning the patience he had been working to develop. That willingness to keep learning may be his most valuable quality. Speaking at the post-match press conference, Hasan said: “One should look to improve their game constantly. I believe that one needs to perform against big teams to make their name. I embrace tough challenges and try to give my all.” His assessment of his dismissal by Jamie Overton was revealing, too. “It was a good ball, but I feel I need to work more on my fitness as my reflexes had gotten slow by then. He had bowled similar deliveries to me prior in the innings, which I was able to dig out.” There is something refreshing about a young batter acknowledging that a good innings could still have been better. Hasan had scored a valuable 79, but rather than being content with the contribution, he identified a possible shortcoming in his fitness and reflexes. Whether that was the decisive factor in his dismissal is difficult to establish, but the willingness to examine his own performance is a positive sign. Pakistan should be careful not to read too much into a handful of promising innings. Hasan remains a work in progress, and there will inevitably be periods when his timing deserts him or his attempts to accelerate come at the expense of his wicket. His relatively small body of work at international level also makes it difficult to know whether the recent improvements will hold up against sustained pressure. What Pakistan can do, however, is provide him with a settled role and enough opportunities to learn from his mistakes. Repeatedly moving him between formats, positions and batting roles risks undoing the progress he has made. If the team management believes he has the attributes to succeed at number six, it must be prepared to accept the occasional failure that comes with developing a player for such a demanding position. Hasan is an intriguing prospect because he has had to reshape his game to meet the requirements of international cricket. A natural opener, he is learning to pace an innings, manage the middle overs and accelerate when the situation demands it. His power gives him a head start, but it is his progress in the less spectacular aspects of batting that will ultimately determine his value to Pakistan. The signs are encouraging, particularly in ODIs, where his ability to consolidate and then change gears could address a longstanding weakness. Yet promise is only a starting point. For Hasan to become a dependable number six, he will need to turn these flashes of maturity into a consistent body of work. Pakistan may have found a diamond in the rough. The challenge now is to give him the time, role and support required to bring out its full value.
